Hon. h. M. MACDONALD (Acting Minister of National Defence): Mr. Speaker, I desire to present the third report of the special committee to whom was referred Bill No. 15 to readjust the representation of the House of Commons. The report is as follows: Wednesday, June 27, 1923.
The special committee, to whom was referred the Bill No. It, an act to readjust the representation in the House of Commons, beg leave to present the following as their third report:
Your committee held several meetings since its appointment on the 22nd of February last. The preparation of the schedules to be annexed to the said Bill was entrusted to sub-committees. The greater number of such sub-committees accomplished considerable work and have, from time to time, reported progress to your committee. It has been found, however, that differences of opinion exist, and your committee have decided that it would be unable to complete the schedules before prorogation.
They therefore have agreed to report back the Bill without amendment, and recommend that a similar committee be appointed at an early period at the next session of Parliament to consider such Bill.
Your committee also recommend that the letters, maps secured from the Department of the Interior and papers produced in the course of its proceedings remain in the possession of the clerk of the committee until the next session of Parliament, and that the same be produced by him at the first regular meeting of the newly-appointed committee.
Your committee also submit herewith a copy of the printed proceedings and evidence taken before them for the information of the House.
All of which is respectfully submitted.
.	Chairman.

MR. HANSON:
1.	Has Charles Ed. Blondin been dismissed as Postmaster at Pierreville, Quebec? If so. when and why?
2.	Is the Government aware that the said C. E. Blondin is a returned soldier who served in the 22nd Battalion and was wounded in the battle of Amiens resulting in the loss of an arm?
3.	Who has been appointed in the place of the said C. E. Blondin, or if no appointment has been made, who has been placed by the department in the position ?
4.	Is the person so placed related to one of the members of Parliament supporting the Government? If so, what is the relationship?

1.	No. Mrs. Boucher was dispossessed of the office on April 20, 1921, without investigation and without any order in council
being passed for that purpose. Mr. Charles Edward Blondin was nominated by the Civil Service Commission for the postmastership of Pierreville on October 8, 1921, but the Department of Justice expressed an opinion on March 2, 1922, that the power of the Postmaster General to remove any postmaster without authority of the Governor-in-Council, had by implication been repealed by the provisions of section 28, sub-section 1 of the Civil Service Act, 1918. Consequently, no vacancy actually existed and the appointment of Mr. Blondin was invalid.
The facts are the following:-
On April 19, 1921, during a by-election in Yamaska County, in which Pierreville is situated, the following instructions were issued by the Honourable P. E. Blondin, Postmaster General:	" Discharge Madame
Boucher, postmistress at Pierreville on the ground that she has permitted strangers to handle the mail on its arrival in the post office on the 11th April and on other dates, contrary to the regulations, and appoint pro tem J. Simeon Letendre".
The stranger referred to was the son of the postmistress, who helped her on occasions to sort the mails, as he had been sworn in for that purpose. The date referred to in the Postmaster General's instructions on which the postmistress permitted a stranger to handle the mails in the post office, namely, April 11, 1921, was two days before the date on which the writ was issued for the by-election in Yamaska County, and for which election Mr. Aime Boucher, the son, was a candidate. There is no evidence that Mr. Aime Boucher helped his mother in the Yamaska post office on or after the date on which the writ was issued for the Yamaska election.
On receipt of the instructions from the Honourable Mr. Blondin, Postmaster General, Madame Boucher was removed from office on April 20, 1921, without any investigation being held, and without any order in Council being passed for that purpose.
Early in 1922, the question was raised as to the validity of this dismissal, and on the case being submitted to the Justice department, the ruling mentioned in answer No. 1, was given, on March 2, 1922. Upon receipt of this ruling, Mrs. Boucher was re-instated in office on March, 7, 1922.
2. The department is aware that Mr. Blondin was a returned soldier and a disability case.
3.	See No. 1.
4. Mrs. Boucher is the mother of Aime Boucher M.P. for Yamaska.

I wish to call the attention of the House and of the government to the continued failure to fill the office of Auditor General of this country. The House realizes-certainly the country does- the supreme importance of this office. The late Auditor General died on the 8th January this year, close to six months ago. Previous to that it is worth observing, he had been ill, and consequently absent from his office since April 1, 1922, or very shortly after this government came into power. His absence from office, of course, I do not mention as attributable at all to the government or as due to any misconduct on their part, but it emphasizes the need of an earlier appointment after his decease. speakeroldname: Hon. W. S. FIELDING (Minister of Finance) :
speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: My right hon. friend asks for a fiat; I do not know what he means. But I do know that the business of the Auditor General's office has been going on-shall I say-fairly satisfactorily. The Acting Auditor General is an old and capable official, and I will give one evidence of his activity: I remind the House that, if not for the first time, certainly for the first time in recent years, immediately after the meeting of parliament the Auditor General's report was laid on the Table. That is a compliment to pay to the Acting Auditor General. Some little time ago when this question was raised I said we were contemplating some legislation respecting the auditing of the country.' That legislation has now been carried, and at a very early day the office of Auditor General will be filled. In the meantime any suggestion that the finances of the country are going to the dogs, that money is being paid out illegally and all that sort of thing, is purely a creation of the right hon. gentleman's imagination.

A favourite expression of the minister's. Hon. GEORGE P. GRAHAM (Minister of Railways and Canals) moved the second reading of Bill No. 244, to amend the Canadian National Railways Act, 1919.
Motion agreed to and the House went into committee on the bill, Mr. Gordon in the chair.
On Section 2-Form, term and amount of securities to be approved.

The apparent effect of the bill-I say the apparent effect, because I dare say my hon. friend will have some answer to the statement-is to change the law only in one particular, namely, as to the right to endorse securities and to pledge the credit of the country. Section 26 of the act already controls the issue of these securities. The main provision here is for government control, and the next thing we have is the guarantee. Subsection 2 of this section reads:
No securities, as defined in this section including in such definition equipment certificates or obligations in any form intended to be issued to the public, shall be issued for the purposes of or by the company or any of the companies designated in the schedule hereto except those approved as to form, terms and amount by the Governor in Council.
That is the first change made by the amendment to section 26, which already provides that the issue of bonds, debentures and securities can only be made with the approval of the Governor in Council. On that point, therefore, there is really no change in the law. The real change is to be found in subsection 3, which reads:
The said securities so approved may be guaranteed by His Majesty and any such guarantee may be in such form and on such terms and conditions as the Governor in Council may determine, and may be signed by the Minister or Acting Minister of Finance on behalf of His Majesty.
This raises in a very serious form the same question that has already been discussed in connection with the act this year providing for railway construction. It was pointed out that under that act the government could make its advances and give its guarantees without including the amount in the estimates and without further authority from parliament. It can be said at least that that act defined the railways to some extent; it afforded a starting point and an ending point. It did not say how the lines were to go, it is true, but apart from that the provision had some definiteness. But here we have a blank cheque given to the government by parliament. Otherwise, why is the change made? Securities were guaranteed before without any trouble, on the authority of parliament given by enactment each year. If this is not a blank cheque, what is it for? If there is one way in which the project of the Canadian National Railways can be ruined it is by causing the people to lose confidence in it through their amazement at the things that are being done. I say that previously we had no difficulty on any question of new commitments, whether of security or of cash. These were new ventures; these were things that ought to be, we thought, considered by parliament. We ought to have some control over the capital issues and the capital activities. We were opposed, not on that score but on the ground that we would not give any details as to the management in such a way as to injure the operations of the companies. To-day the government not only take the stand which they formerly condemned, that is in favour of independence of management, they not only want independence of management, but they want the country's credit absolutely removed from the control of parliament. If there ever was a time when this proposition should be looked into closely and strictly that time is now. My hon. friends opposite say they have taken the National system out of politics. Why, they have thrown it into politics. I should like to know any better way of making this a political matter than appointing a purely political board. That is what we have. Keep it out of politics! Why, it is in politics now. Does anyone suggest that the Premier could give Mr. Sinclair any hints in the game of practical politics, as applied in connection with the operation of the line down in Nova Scotia? Does he think he could teach Mr. Dawson,

C. N. R.-Securities
manager of Reform campaigns in British Columbia, anything about practical politics in that province? Again, does he think he could teach Mr. Gough anything about practical politics in Ontario? Why, the only claims of these gentlemen to appointment were that they were good political hacks. Ihat is all, and nothing else. Now we are to have a combination with this political railway board under which the government will have the right to pledge the -credit of the country to any securities that the government's political friends may see fit to put forward and the government may see fit to approve of. If it is not for the purpose of getting this large over-holding right why have this legislation? No difficulty has been experienced in the past. What is the reason for the legislation to-day?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: If jt were not for the fact that my hon. friend is usually in a very genial frame of mind I would be tempted to apply to him that quotation with which we are all familiar, "Suspicion haunts the guilty mind." My hon. friend has read into this bill things which are not there, and which can only be carried into it by an extraordinary Right of the imagination. I am not going to discuss the political question at all. This is a business proposition, and I am going to confine my remarks entirely to the bill. My hon. friend has been wandering away from the question.
Not very far.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
He wants to know
whether Mr. A., Mr. B., or Mr. C. js a worthy man for the position. He has no right to reflect upon the character of these men. Those of them I know personally are high-minded gentlemen. He mentioned in particular Mr. Sinclair. There is no more honourable man in the Dominion of Canada than Mr. Sinclair, and the suggestion that he will not faithfully and honourably discharge his duty as a commissioner for the National railways is entirely unwarranted. I am sure that on reflection my hon. friend will see-and the same remark applies to the other commissioners-that what he has said is not justified. Now this bill-and it is only with the bill that I am concerned-says that no securities shall be issued by the National Railway Company or the subsidiaries connected with it except by the consent of the Governor General in Council. The hon. gentleman says that is already provided for. Possibly it is. In that case the worst that can be said of this legislation, as I remarked the other day. is that it is surplusage. If, however, the 
power is required at any time it is there. Will my hon. friend tell me what harm can come by stating definitely that under no conditions shall that board issue securities without coming to the government? What is wrong with such a provision as that? My hon. friend says the power is not needed. Whether we have it or not is debatable-I am not sure that we do have that power already,-but in any event what harm will be done by this legislation? That is the first purpose of the bill. Can anybody object to it? Surely not for a moment. I do not know on what ground the hon. gentleman bases hio argument. How in the world can he connect this bill with some of the things he is talking about I fail to discover.
The next purpose of the bill is that the government may issue guarantees. This measure does not give the government power to do anything except to guarantee securities that can be legally issued. Now, if the Canadian National Railway Company has any power, given by this parliament, to issue a security it is better that that security should have the approval of the government and <hus sell at a good price. That is the whole story. This bill does not give the government power to guarantee any issue that is not already authorized by parliament. I do not expect the power is going to be used to any extent at all. My hon. friend is imagining difficulties. I think it was the leader of the Opposition who said that the old borrowing powers had been extinguished. Well,
I am advised that even that is a debatable matter. I am advised that some of these outstanding companies, subsidiaries of the Canadian National Railways, are still distinct entities and have powers and rights of their own. We certainly do not intend that these companies shall issue any bonds. There will be no guarantee given on any bond issue that is not authorized by this parliament. What greater assurance could my hon. friend ask? Now, they say this legislation is not necessary-

What does the hon.
gentleman mean by the expression " authorized by parliament?" Suppose this bill passes, what will the company have to do to get a bond issue authorized by parliament?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: If they have no legal authority to issue a bond, if they are not authorized by this parliament to do so, there will be no bond issue.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Does my right hon.
friend say they have not the power now? If so that ends it. If they have no legal right to issue bonds there will be no guarantee.
Assuming they have the right what will they have to do, after this bill passes, to get an unlimited bond issue?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: My right hon. friend is now reversing his own argument. Only a moment ago he was claiming that this power did not exist.
Let my hon. friend take it any way he likes.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: My right hon. friend can have it either way, but not both ways. He has already stated that in the case of these companies the borrowing powers are extinguished. If so there can be no bond issue. How does my right hon. friend get away from that argument. I have already given my hon. friends an assurance in that respect. What more do they want? My right hon. friend thinks there is no need of this power at all. I will give him an illustration showing to the contrary. To-day there is a requirement of the Canadian National Railway for $15,000,000 on equipment bonds. I am advised that there is no authority under the law to guarantee these bonds. It is the only security that I contemplate will be guaranteed. I am told there is no authority under the existing law for the Governor in Council to guarantee these bonds' and if they are to be issued, and they must be issued lawfully, it is better that they should bear the guarantee of the government of Canada and command a good price on the market than that they should have to be sold at a sacrifice. That is the whole story; there is nothing else behind it in the world. The suggestion of my hon. friends that this is a scheme devised for new guarantees for new and unauthorized securities is without any foundation whatever. That I can assure my hon. friends in all sincerity and good faith.

I doubt

and, I confess
it, with some feeling of despair-whether I can succeed in convincing the minister, but I should like to convince the House. I am not certain that I can do that but I am going to do the best I can. Of the state of the law I do not think there is any doubt, but it does not matter a particle whether there is or not, so far as the merits of this legislation go. It is not always an easy matter to make a legal proposition clear. Fortunately, in this case it does not matter which end of the dilemma the hon. gentleman takes, not in the least.
He says, first of all, that he wants to secure government control of bond issues of the Canadian National Railway Company, and I as'k the House to remember there is only one such company which was created by the statutes of 1919, chapter 13. That company has included in its system other companies. Those companies had their own charters from parliament and their own powers, the parent company gets no power from those. That is my opinion. I do not care whether it is accepted or not, its acceptance or otherwise does not matter in the least. We are dealing in this bill with the parent company and no other, hon. members only need to read the bill to see that. The bill deals with the parent company and only the parent company. I say the parent company never had power to issue a dollar of security without the approval of the Governor in Council, and never issued a dollar, and how in the world the most elementary first-form student in the government can think of anything else I do not know. I do not think any of them do think anything else, and I will say what I really think in a minute. Section 26 which starts this way-
The company-
The company is defined in the act. Nobody suggests that the company means anything except the Canadian National Railway Company.
The company may with the approval of the Governor in Council issue bonds.
How can anything be more specific? It is just the language that is used here. This says that no security can be issued unless the form, and so on, are approved by the Governor-in-Council It may be asked, why is this put in? It is just put in as a smoke screen to get the second section through no other reason at all. There is no more reason for that first clause than there is for the hon. minister to take an excerpt from a novel and put it there. It is merely as something to introduce the second section. The government thought it would look just a little too naked, and the object would be a little too clear if the second section appeared there alone. Let us come to the second section. The second section says that once they get the approval of the Governor-in-Council, which they always had to get, the government might guarantee the bonds. I have never objected to the government having power to guarantee the bonds. I do not object to it. I do not think there is the slightest need of it. The government has the power to-day to guarantee the bonds. If anybody has any doubt about it, I will accept his doubt and assume they have not the power. Does the minister
C. N. R.-Securities

not know we have to guarantee them over and over again? Why did he not tell the House last session of the brilliant sale he made in New York of government guaranteed bonds? Does he imagine the counsel for the purchasers did not examine the authority of the guarantee, to be sure it was legal? Why, of course they did, and there has never been a question raised that I have heard that they had the power to guarantee. But let me assume they have not the power, that somebody in the Justice department or in the Railway department has told them there may be a little doubt about having the power to guarantee. I will assume he is right. Here is what they are doing. They are taking the power to do it, without including the amount of the guarantee in the estimates, something which they never did before. That is the whole effect of the legislation. Just add to it that they have to place the amount of the guarantee in the estimates, and the government will reject the bill, and that is what they do not want to do. Why should this be? The minister did not mention it. Why does he not want that? Why did he not put it in the estimates? I do not see the object unless he wants to make the estimates appear low to the country and take carte blanche himself to give any guarantees he likes. The minister thinks it will be more advantageous to himself, his government or his party. I do not know why. The minister says we are very suspicious. Well, what is an opposition for?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: To be reasonable.

Yes, to be reasonable. I will take the reason from the mouth of the minister himself. He called attention to the absence of this in a bill four years ago. I am not sure that he himself did it, but I am pretty sure that he did. I know the Prime Minister did. I know we acceded to it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: What restrictions will the hon. member put in?
That the amount of the guarantee shall be put in and voted by parliament.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I will deal with that in a minute.

It is a wonder the minister did not mention it. I am prepared to let it go through, if that restriction is applied.
J hat is all I am fighting for. Why should the minister not accept it?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Go on and finish and I will answer.
The minister might tell me now.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
We are getting back to
the old trouble. I am asked, why should we not put the guarantee in the estimates? Because it has never been the practice of parliament to put guarantees in the estimates.
Oh, oh.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: In the annual vote that we make there is a provision including guarantees within the limitation of that vote; but the general powers to guarantee the bonds of the company are not usually expressed; and in the estimates there is no departure from the custom. The only exception you will find is in the regular vote for the railways, where the sum is voted, and you may apply that vote by cash or guarantee Or any other way. But the statement that the guarantees of the Canadian Northern have always been voted in the estimates is absolutely at variance with the facts.

The minister is simply
wrong.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I am not wrong. My
hon. friend will find that every act to guarantee the bond of a railway company has been an act in itself, and not shown in the estimates'. And that is reason and common sense. What are the purposes of the bill? The hon. member says we have the power already to prevent the issue of bonds, without the consent of the Governor in Council. That may be debatable. I am advised there is a doubt about that. But assuming there is no doubt about it, will the hon. member tell me what harm is done when we make assurance doubly sure by making it clear this railway company shall not issue any securities without the knowledge and approval of the Governor in Council. What is wrong with that? Nothing. We come to the guarantee. We can only guarantee bonds which are lawfully issued, and if any bond is to be lawfully issued by the Canadian National railway, that is the bond of the government of Canada. If it is issued simply as the bond of the Canadian National Railway, it has only a diminished value. Since we are going to be responsible for it, why should we not make it in a form and condition which will enable us to- sell it at the best price? That is the whole story.
I will cite a case in point. My hon. friend says we have all the power. We have not. I am advised that with regard to the Canadian National equipment which the commission require, we have not the power to supply it

C. N. R.-Securities
without this bill. Without this bill the bonds would be sold in the market without the guarantee.

To a lot of what the
minister has said, no reply is necessary.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Hear, hear.

I do not care whether
he is right or wrong; that is as to having the power to guarantee the equipment bonds. If he is right it serves my purpose just as well. If he is wrong, if he feels he needs additional power, I do not object to give it to him at all. But when he says this is what has always been done -unlimited of guarantee-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Not unlimited power.
Where is the limit?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: They can only guarantee the bonds where lawfully issued and the onus will be on the party issuing them.

If they should issue
bonds for 85,000,000, have they not the power to issue them?

speechtext: No.
Where is the restraint?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: They can only guarantee a bond that is lawfully issued and the proposal to issue $5,000,000 of bonds without legislative authority certainly would not come within the provisions of the act.

Without any legislative
authority?-Have they not just as much legislative authority to issue bonds for $5,000000,000 as for $5,000,000?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No, the legislative authority will apply in each case. There is no power to issue for $5,000,000,000.

There is no special authority for any bond here-none whatever- no authority for a bond for $1,000. And there is just as much authority for a bond of $5,000,000,000. They have power to issue such bonds to-day, if they have power to issue anything. Consequently there is no limit here to the power of the guarantee. The whole point is this-and I ask the House not to be confused by the introduction of any other matter- whether the amount should be in the estimates or not. The minister says it never has been in the estimates, and he says we have given railway guarantees without it. The latter statement is right, but we never gave a guarantee to the Canadian National without it, and this bill is to guarantee the Canadian National railway bonds. Certainly,
every time when we guaranteed the bonds of private companies we did not include it in the estimates.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: My hon. friend is changing his ground.

Not at all, and no one in this House thinks I am. What I say is this, that we have always included in the estimates, our guarantees as well as our cash advances. The minister cannot point to a dollar that was ever guaranteed the Canadian National that we failed to put right in the Estimates, so that the country knew the amount. I want to know why the minister wants that changed. What is the effect of all this? The minister, if this legislation passes, can guarantee just at his will, and the country will have no knowledge whatsoever, that is, in compact and unified form, of what the country's commitments to our National railways are. Instead of making cash advances each year to the railways and putting that in the Estimates if this legislation passes, the company can issue bonds, and the minister will guarantee them.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is nonsense.

He will do that. Why should we pass legislation to let him do nonsense whether he wants it or not? I do not attribute lack of intelligence to the minister, but he cannot suggest honestly that he should have power to do that.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I say that we would have no power to do it.
The minister is hopeless, if he takes a position of that sort.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I know he is.
Why would he not have power? Will he tell me anything he has not power to do if this passes? And then I will suggest something a minute afterwards.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The right hon. gentleman had better make his minute-afterwards suggestion now.

All right. I will suggest the alternative now. Supposing the company issue a $15,000,000 equipment bond and the minister guarantees that. He says that if this passes, the company will have power to do that and the minister will have power. to guarantee it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Not by this legislation. The company have the power already. All we ask is the power to guarantee the bond.

I am not bothering about that. I am not asking about that. If this legislation passes, the company will have

C. N. R.-Securities

power to issue such a bond, and the minister will have power to guarantee it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The power to issue is not in this legislation; the power to guarantee is.
What is the difference? There is not a particle of difference. I am afraid the minister is trying to mislead the House.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is unkind.

I will put the matter in this way. They have the power now to issue bonds, and if this legislation passes, the government has power to guarantee them. Supposing, instead of issuing bonds to cover equipment, they issued bonds to cover the deficit for the year-suppose they have a deficit of 810,000,000, and that they issue a bond for $50,000,000 instead of $15,000,000. The bond covers equipment and deficit. Does the minister say that if this legislation passes, the company will have power to do that, and he will have power to guarantee the bond?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I have some difficulty in understanding what my right hon. friend is driving at. I cannot understand that we have power to guarantee anything that is not already authorized by parliament. The Canadian National Railway Act does not deal specifically with equipment bonds. This is only an illustration. Equipment bonds are not issued in the usual way; they are not covered by an ordinary guarantee, and therefore it is desirable, if we want those bonds to be sold at the best market price, that they should be put before the public in the best possible form. If this bill does not pass, what will happen? The Canadian National Railways will issue $15,000,000 worth of equipment bonds on their own credit. They are a good class of bond. If they are issued on the New York market, they will not, perhaps, benefit very much by a guarantee. If they are issued on the Canadian market, the Canadian government guarantee will be helpful. The question is: Which of the two ways should we, who have the responsibility of dealing with the matter, pursue-put the bonds on the market in such a shape that they will command the highest price, or issue them with the full knowledge that they are going to be sold at a sacrifice price?
Why does the Minister keep saying that, instead of answering the question in the form in which he asked for it himself? I do not object to his guaranteeing the bonds. Can I repeat that too often?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No.

I showed, I think, to everyone who wants to understand and who approaches the matter impartially, that either as the act now is, or as it will be when amended-I do not care which-the company can issue any bonds so long as the government approves.
Could they issue a bond for a deficit?
Certainly they could, with the approval of the government, issue a bond to pay their debts.
A great bond!

With the approval of the government, they can issue a bond to pay their debts. That would be the least objectionable. Supposing they issued a bond for equipment to any extent whatever, say to $100,000,000, does the Minister suggest that they would not have power to do that?
It seems clear to me. My right hon. friend-
Why cannot the Minister answer that, " yes " or " no "?
If the right hon. member does not want my answer, all right.
Let him answer anyway he likes, but I do not understand why he cannot answer, " yes " or " no ". The Minister is trying to confuse the House over this bill.
My right hon. friend is trying to confuse the House, but he is not making a good shot at that.

If this bill passes, the company can issue bonds to any extent at all, and the government do not need to come to parliament and show what they are going to guarantee for a single year. All I ask is that the latter be conceded, and I give
12 noon this House warning now, that no such power has ever before been given to a government in relation to our roads and no such power should be given. It is going to tend to confuse the country and parliament as to the actual financial history of the railways. It is going to change the whole method of presenting to the country the record of our railways. That is the purpose of it. Let hon. members read page 33 of the Estimates for last year, or practically the same page of the Estimates for this year. Let them read how the Estimates read in previous years, showing that the amount every time included not only the cash advances, but the guarantees. That had to be done.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
No.

The Minister says, " no ". It did. There is no use in telling the Minister anything.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I am afraid not.
Let the Minister show me a dollar that was guaranteed that was not included in the Estimates. If he gets up, he will likely go back to private roads.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I will go back to the facts.

Let him adhere to the Canadian National Railways and tell me of a dollar that was guaranteed or a dollar that was advanced that was not included in the Estimates and authorized in the Estimates by parliament.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The annual appropriation to make up what is estimated to be the possible deficit of the Canadian National Railways includes the statement that the advances to be made may be by loan, or by cash, or in any other way. It does not have reference to transactions like this at all. The right hon. gentleman got wrong first, and he has been wandering around ever since and trying to get right.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No.
What?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Go on.

I do not know what is wrong with the minister. (Reading):
(c)	Interest and sinking funds on notes, securities or obligations.
(d)	Principal and interest of maturing or matured loans secured or unsecured.
(e)	Construction and betterments.
Is that the annual deficit on operations?

Guarantees of securities of the Grand Trunk Pacific.
Everything is included, and the whole of the Estimates there includes what the government does by cash or guarantee in relation to anyone of them.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The right hon. gentleman began by getting wrong as to the relation between Estimates and railway appropriations. He began with a statement, made with a great flourish of trumpets, that previously the appropriations for these various purposes had been shown in the Estimates, and he flourished the Estimates. Then also with a modest flourish of trumpets, we pointed out that millions have been provided for railway aid without being shown in the Estimates. When he was beaten on that ground, he shifted around to the other.

The minister knows right well and this House knows, that I have discussed from the beginning the Canadian National Railways and nothing else. There has been no shifting of ground, and I will not let anyone, who does not want to be, be confused by what the minister is trying to say about my shifting ground. I have referred to that and to that alone, and from the beginning stated I had no reference to cur conduct as related to private roads.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: My hon. friend did not make any qualification at the beginning.
None was needed.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: When I stated that appropriations for railway subsidies were not shown in the Estimates, he said I was mistaken; then he revised that and said he did not know. We have on the order paper today a resolution authorizing the loan of $10000,000 to the harbour commission of Montreal. We have voted these appropriations again and again and not one is shown in the Estimates, and the hon. gentleman knows it. Therefore his contention that every appropriation is shown in the Estimates is absolutely wrong.
I never so contended.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Another point. The Railway department, following the usual practice, contemplated the issue of these bonds-as they had power to do-and they did not include them in the estimates sent to us. But they had the power to issue these fifteen million dollars worth of bonds, and all we do by this bill is to say: Instead of issuing these bonds in the name of the Canadian National Railways, and selling them at a sacrifice, you shall have endorsed on them the guarantee of the government of Canada, and so sell them at a good price. That is the whole story.

I think the minster's effort is getting plain. I have argued this on the basis of National Railway appropriations; in respect to other matters the question is not affected at all. If in the past we have had advances for harbour improvements and the like authorized by statute and not included in the Estimates, then there is going to be no confusion in making comparisons; but in relation to our railways, from this time on

Securities

there will be kept out of the Estimates those things that were always in before. It is just as plain to the minister as to anybody else, but he has got to make a fight to get this through. He is determined to exclude these from the Estimates where they have always been in relation to our National Railways. If he thinks equipment is not included in supplies for railways, all right, put it in; but put it in where it has always been before, and where it ought to be in the Estimates. Let him amend his Supplementary Estimates and put it there, and I will raise no objection at all. Now it is plain what the minister wants.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It is, but it is not plain what my hon. friend wants.

I wonder if we connot agree upon some things without any unnecessary heat. After all, there ought to be no real object in anyone trying to mislead this House upon what is really a matter very important to public business. In connection with the railways we embarked upon something which is entirely new. It did not have anything to do with railway subsidies for private companies. It had absolutely nothing to do with advances to the Montreal Harbour Commission. It was something which, as I say, was not only entirely novel, but it was the particular business of the country; it was something that we were doing eurselves. It was not any question of how many thousand dollars per mile this House had authorized the government to guarantee for the Canadian Pacific Railway; it was our own business, the management and running of our own lines. We went about it under the act of 19,19. We had extracts read the other day from the debate upon that act, and it was shown that the point had been raised under the statutes of 1919, that parliamentary control of capital account ought to be maintained. Why, the present Prime Minister said that the last vestige of parliamentary control would disappear if that was not done, and the then government very cheerfully agreed at once; they never expected anything else.
My hon. friend says that this has never been in the Estimates. I am sure he does not mean it. I want to give my friend every credit for sincerity just as long as it is possible for me to do so, and I think what he means is that the ordinary guarantees of privately-owned railway bonds did not appear in the Estimates. I tell the House that I believe absolutely that not one single guarantee was given, so far as I know, that was not included in the bulk amount voted by parliament. Does my hon. friend dispute that statement?
I Mr. Meiehen.l

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Go on.
I should like to get this thing cleared up, to get rid of the mists and come down to facts. If my bon. friend disputes that statement, now is the time for him to do so.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Go on.
Very good, there is no dispute.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I did not say that.

Well, it cannot be disputed. Why, my hon. friend himself shows how it cannot be disputed. This year a different plan has been adopted. He himself a few minutes ago, speaking on this very question of the Estimates, says that this year the fifteen million dollars is not included in his seventy-two million dollars. We had an equipment guarantee last year-it was included without any such bill as this.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: My hon. friend is wrong. We had no guarantee last year.
Did not my hon. friend guarantee the equipment securities that he reported to the House last session and sold in New York?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: They were not equipment securities. My hon. friend is all wrong in the facts.
What kind of securities were they?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: They were securities of the Canadian Northern Railway at one stage, afterwards they were securities of the Dominion government, upon which we borrowed one hundred million dollars.
I was not speaking of those securities, but it makes no difference.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It does.
Were there any equipment bonds guaranteed last year?

It makes no
difference whether it is equipment or whether it is any other kind of security that is guaranteed, the principle is exactly the same. They may not have been equipment securities, but they were railway securities, and they were guaranteed without such legislation as this, simply because the amount of the guarantee was included in the Estimates.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
No, my recollection is that it was not included in the Estimates.

C. N. R.-Securities

I am quite sure my hon. friend will find that they were. If he could do so without their being included in the Estimates, however, what earthly justification is there for this bill? The whole idea of this measure is to see that the securities are sold properly. Were not the securities sold properly at that time? Did not my hon. friend get a good price for them? Of course, they were in the Estimates. The wording was carefully worked out to cover all these things, and my hon. friend practically admits it in his own statement when he says that this fifteen million dollars is not included in this main vote. Those having been included in the main vote, he had a right to guarantee them. I ask the government to look at page 31 of their own Estimates of this year and ask themselves whether that means anything except that power is taken for the purpose of guaranteeing securities of all classes. Why, we can even guarantee securities for operating deficits; it is not done, I know, but it could be done. The vote says, "Acquisition of property, materials and supplies," and to wind it up you have an omnibus provision, "guarantees of securities." The government said: We ask for all this and we agree to keep ourselves within the limit that parliament sets upon it. Then the estimate becomes a statute thus making the provisions enacted perfectly valid and binding. In fact that is how the business has always been done. .
I am at a loss to understand my hon. friend's position. Bonds and securities have been successfully sold in the past without this act; he himself has done it. Yet he tells us that the whole object of this act is to enable the sale of securities. Why, his own record shows that that is [nonsense, that his argument is pure piffle. This question of giving a blank cheque to the administration is a novel thing. We were told in connection with the construction programme that one reason why this unlimited power should be given was that works were contemplated which would run over more than one year and that the only proper thing to do was to arrange for the whole matter at once. That was the only argument that amounted to anything in connection with that bill, and that argument does not apply here at all. The only possible object of this legislation is to enable the government to put themselves in a position to do just what they please. What the Minister of Railways said is quite right, that there is a distinction between the right to issue a security and the
right to guarantee, and it is also true that under this provision the government should only guarantee bonds which may be legally issued by the corporation. But under the statutory borrowing powers of the company they may raise $75,000 a mile on their whole mileage. I forget the exact figures of the existing bonded indebtedness per mile; the Minister of Railways will know it-but I venture to say that the exact amount of securities issued is much below $75,000 per mile.
I think that is true.

Of course it is true; the minister admits it. Up to the extent, then, of $75,000 per mile the right to issue exists and the right to guarantee is given. There is no limit so far as the issue of bonds for equipment purpose is concerned.

Is my hon. friend clear that the Canadian National Railway Company could issue securities against the Canadian Northern system? Legally and technically the Canadian Northern system has never been brought into the Canadian National system.
I am surprised to hear that; I understood, the last time this subject was discussed, that we now had proper co-ordination.

There are certain difficulties concerning a portion of the stock which the government is taking steps to get possession of. It had not got the possession yet, and legally and technically the Canadian Northern is not, as I am advised, a part of the Canadian National Railway system. That is why I asked the question.

I think the act which deals with the question of borrowing powers makes that perfectly clear. If there is any doubt about it, I do not see how securities have been sold in the past. They have been sold under this act and they have been regarded by very eminent New York counsel as perfectly good securities. The act says that the company may with the approval of the Governor in Council issue bonds and debentures, then it takes out from the application of the computation of $75,000 a mile the government railways, but it leaves everything else in. The schedule specifically mentions the Canadian Northern and a great many other companies.

That would be when they are in.
C. N. R.-Securities
There is no limit, except the proper business limit; there is no legal limit to the issue of securities against equipment. The equipment itself forms the security.
The Government by an estimate, I think, provided that twenty-five per cent of the balance could be issued by the company.

In this legislation we are getting away from the provision of these things in the Estimates, and the fact is that there will be no limit. Are we going to do something which was excused the other day only because it covered a three-year programme and the work could not be done all at once? Are we going to do something which changes all our previous practice? Are we going to write this blank cheque to the government?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
My hon. friend began his observations by saying he was unable to understand my position. Well, I think I can understand his; he got in wrong at the beginning and he is now trying to maintain an utterly indefensible position. What is the issue? This resolution does not create the power to issue any securities; not a doliar can be issued under this bill. If there is an outstanding authority granted by parliament to the Canadian National Railway Company to issue bonds, then in the judgment of the Governor in Council those bonds may be guaranteed. That is the essential feature. The hon. member for West York (Sir Henry Drayton) and the right hon. leader of the Opposition (Mr. Meighen) say that every obligation that is assumed, every guarantee and every appropriation, must be shown in the Estimates; that is the great principle they are struggling for. Then my hon. friend in vain tried to bolster up that argument by saying that a year or two ago we issued an equipment security guarantee; why not do jt now? Well, the answer is that we did not issue an equipment security guarantee then; l<e is materially wrong in his facts. Then he says that we issued guaranteed securities in New York at another time and asks why we should not do so now. We issued securities which were guaranteed by act of the parliament of Canada in the name of the Canadian Northern Railway Company. There was a law providing for it, and the issue was made under the provisions of that law. My hon. friend djd the same thing a year or two ago and did not show it in the Estimates. He issued a guarantee for the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company and for the Canadian

Northern Railway Company, and he dad not show it in the Estimates; he did not do the thing he now says is essential.
Will my hon. friend be kind enough to give particulars of any guarantee we made that was not shown in the Estimates?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I say he issued two loans -and I am not criticising him-guaranteed in the qity of New York, one for the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company and one for the Canadian Northern Railway Company, and to the best of my knowledge and belief neither was shown in the Estimates. It is not. customary to show guarantees in the Estimates. So in relation to all these material facts my hon. friend is wrong. Now, the whole story is this-and I repeat: not a dollar cf bonds can be issued under this legislation. If there is already an authority to issue bonds, is it better that they should go on the market at a sacrifice price, or is it better that we should put the endorsation of the government upon them and sell at the best possible price?
I want to tell my hon. friend that so far as these Canadian government bonds he refers to are concerned, they were included in the total amount of the Estimates, and we never exceeded it.
Never what?
They were included in the Estimates. It is true they were not included by name.
Oh, oh.

What is the " oh " for? We do not ask in this case that it be included by name; we simply ask that the country know what the total payment is, that is all. My hon. friend makes a splurge about the matter of equipment, but so far as that is concerned it does not make the slightest difference. These loans were made under previously existing powers, and there was no trouble. The whole truth is that the minister wants to get away from this limitation. What is the use of talking about wanting to issue bonds so that they will sell well; they were sold well before. That has nothing to do with it. I started out to give some reasons for this change, and I could give others, as I am sure my hon. friend could himself give them. For example, was there anything but a political reason for the appointment of the gentleman who now represents the city of Quebec on the board?

speechtext: What has that to do with this matter?

Everything;
they are the people with whom you have to deal; people in your own class, in your own scale.

speechtext: The discussion of the board of directors at this stage is out of order. The matter under consideration is the question of guarantees. Shall section 2 carry?

As I understand it, the purpose of this act is to give the government power to issue these equipment certificates or obligations without the consent of parliament.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The power is there already. All this gives is the right to guarantee.
This will be done without the consent of parliament?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: This is the consent of parliament now.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Oh no, no.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I assure my hon. friend that this legislation creates no power to issue securities. If any security already authorized by parliament is to be issued, the government may in their wisdom guarantee it; that is the whole story. It guarantees nothing in the future; the legislation is confined entirely to authority already issued by parliament. We cannot grant a guarantee on anything not already authorized by parliament.

With respect to the financial railway commitments of this session, as I understand it we are committed in the main estimates to $73,000,000 for deficits and so forth. We are committed by the bill of the other day to $28,000,000 for construction. We are making a committal now for $15,000,000 or more for equipment, making a total of committals in respect of the National Railways for this year of $116,000,000, part of which will be expended over a period of approximately three years. That is, I think, a correct statement. The House should keep it in mind that unquestionably next year we shall be asked to make other commitments in the matter of extensions, equipment, and so forth, so that while the expenditure may be over three years, during those three years other commitments will be added. My point is simply this and I wish to make it clear that this session the parliament of Canada is committing the country to an expenditure of $116,000,000 to cover deficits, equipment bonds and new construction of branch lines for the National Railways.

Sub-section 3 of section 2 of the bill reads as follows:
The said securities so approved may be guaranteed by His Majesty and any such guarantee may be in such form and on such terms and conditions as the Governor in Council may determine-
And so forth. We have no control over the policy and administration of the National Railways Company. Now, as a matter of fact the success of an issue of securities, more particularly in the case of a railway system of this kind, depends upon the manner and method of administration. We have heard it said often in the last year or two that we should give these railways a free hand. Is parliament to be debarred from any say as to these expenditures? It was not public ownership that got the railways into the condition where they show such large deficits, it was private ownership. What is going to become of responsible government in this country if we are to continue to spend money on these railways at the rate we are doing? Just think of it, a deficit of $73,000,000; $28,000,000 to be expended on branch lines, and $15,000,000 to be spent upon equipment, a total of $116,000,000. Compare that expenditure upon the railway system alone and then recall the fact that in 1896 the entire Dominion expenditure amounted to only $36,000,000. It is all very well to talk about giving the railways a free hand but no country in the world would confer upon a railway company such powers as we propose to grant without adequate parliamentary control. At the rate charges have been accumulating on these railways I do not know how matters are going to end. And yet some people talk of the necessity of giving the National Railways a free hand. Now, we have these deficits to which I have referred, and the expenditure of the railway system is piling up at a rapid

C. N. R.-Securities
rate. It should be borne in mind that extravagance in operation is likely to seriously affect railway securities when they are placed upon the market. Is there ground for the assertion that extravagance has characterized the management of our railways? I think there is. For example, a sum of from $80,000 to $100,000 has been expended in fixing up a private car to enable the directors to travel all over Canada. I contend this is extravagance which should not exist, and it does not exist in the operation of railways under private management. I am friendly to public ownership, but I confess I am very much alarmed at the extravagance of the directors in conducting our national railways. Giving them a free hand, if carried to its logical conclusion, will bankrupt the national railways and, speaking metaphorically, drive them into the poor house. Look at the position in which the great railways in the United States find themselves. They are short of rolling stock, short of equipment in every respect, and their securities are not selling at nearly the former prices. Shaughnessy and Van Horne are said to have made a great success of railway administration in the United States a great many years ago, and afterwards they were identified with the Canadian Pacific Railway in this country. But not even the genius of a Shaughnessy or a Van Home could have made of the Canadian Pacific the success it has been had it not been for the liberal "handout" given by this country. Of course there was also efficiency in operation. I doubt whether either of those railway magnates could make a success of the Canadian National Railways under the extravagant methods that now seem to prevail. The issue of bonds and securities by the Canadian National Railways should be made a matter of consideration and approval by the Railway Commission. What was the object of creating such a body if it was not to deal with matters of this kind. It is folly to talk about giving the management of our railways a free hand when there is such a lack of economy and efficient control. If parliament is going to give the management a free hand it will be a ruinous policy. We shall not, however, see any improvement until we return to the system of responsible government and parliamentary authority for expenditures.

I want to take every
step in my power to prevent this kind of legislation going through unguarded. I think the House as a whole now understands the attempts at concealment. There is only one thing in issue. It is not any question of the amount of the liability we are involved in,
it is not a question of the powers we are granting, it is merely a question of whether we are going to depart from the custom we have observed from the commencement of the National Railways, of including the country's commitments in the Estimates. That is the whole question, and I do not think anybody can be honestly convinced to the contrary. When the same question was up before, in connection with new construction, the ministers had a better chance. They said, " Oh, this is for three years and we might not have enough in the Estimates to last just over the end of the fiscal year, and a contractor might have to stop," as if that would not apply to any other public work just the same. But they managed to confuse hon. members, and I have thought they must have had a good laugh in council, when they got through, over the way they did it. They cannot use that argument in this case, consequently they have been less successful. I therefore move, seconded by Mr. Tolmie:
That there be added to subsection 3 of section 2 the following words:
Provided that before any guarantee is given the amount of same shall be included each year in the estimates and be voted by parliament.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The principle involved
is scarcely worthy of a moment's consideration. The right hon. gentleman takes the ground that every appropriation and every obligation for the year undertaken by the government of Canada must be set forth in the estimates.
I did not say that.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
If the right hon. gentleman did not say that it is the substance of his argument. That is a departure from the practice of parliament. We do not set forth every obligation. There are many cases-I have already given illustrations, I can furnish many more-where appropriations are made by special act and are not set forth in the estimates. It makes no earthly difference whether they are voted in the estimates or are authorized by special act; the essence of the whole thing is that these obligations cannot be assumed without the vote of the House; and whether you have it on this page or that page, in this blue book or that blue book, what earthly difference does it make to the people of Canada? The obligations are assumed on parliamentary authority and are set forth and shown in the public accounts. There have been cases again and again-there always have been under the administration of hon. gentlemen opposite, there were such cases under our administration, and there will be in the future-when it is deemed right and
Post Office Act

proper to provide for special appropriations in acts of parliament. You may lay down the rule that in every case the amount must be shown in the Estimates but I say it is a matter of no earthly importance to the parliament or the people of Canada so long as the rule is recognized of parliamentary control, and that no appropriation can be made unless it is made by this House. That is the essence of the whole thing. That is the principle for which we stand.

On section 1-Postage rates on certain newspapers and periodicals reduced from li cents to li cents.

minister might explain this section.

The explanation was
given yesterday. Summarized it is a changing of the maximum postal rates on periodicals from li to li cents per pound.

This is a lot more important than appears on the surface. The minister did give a fairly full explanation the other day. The rate was formerly very low entailing a tremendous loss to the country for the carriage of newspapers; and it is only fair that the House should know-which the minister did not say-that this loss necessarily was borne by the whole country, except the few who got the benefit of it. While it is true in a slight degree that the small newspapers get some benefit, the newspapers which get the real benefit are the great big newspapers that travel all over the Dominion, that go out of Montreal and Toronto and circulate from end to end of the country. The Dominion, as a matter of fact, was shouldering a heavy obligation in carrying newspapers, entailing, I cannot recall just how much, but running into hundreds of thousands-yes, running into millions of dollars; I am pretty sure I am right on that point, the minister should be able to tell us. So that it really amounted to a subsidy. The late government started to correct that state of affairs, and by a graduated scale we provided-and parliament accepted the provision -that the rate should go up to, I think, li cents per pound. My recollection was, and the minister confirmed it yesterday, that even then we had not overtaken the loss by any means, and that it cost a great deal more to distribute than li cents per pound.

Mr. MEIGHEN I appreciate the importance atached to my words by the Chair, because certainly all ought to hear them. This government has evidently submitted to importunities and proposes to go back, not all but part of the road, and leave the rate at li cents. I do not know what is involved in this li cents. not to the small papers-the amount that they are interested in, while of course it is something, is very little. The great benefit goes to the big newspapers. Let me emphasize this. The small newspaper is really hurt, I would think, by the low rate, for the reason that the field of the small newspaper is then more easily invaded by the large. The large newspaper gets into the small newspaper's field at the public expense, because of the cheap rate, and consequently curtails the circulation of the small newspaper. Is the minister not doing an injustice rather than a favour to the small newspapers? Ostensibly, perhaps, the small newspaper proprietor will think: "I would like to get my paper out as cheaply as I can, more cheaply than actual cost," but he will find his field more easily invaded by the big paper. According to the law, I understand the rate of postage is the same for a long distance as for a short. I am pretty sure I am right in that. Therefore a ne.wspapr is carried from Montreal to Vancouver at the same rate as that for which the proprietor of a small newspaper gets his paper carried perhaps, a ride of eight miles. Thus, the more you go below the cost, the greater the advantage to the big newspaper in its competition with the smaller one, particularly in view of the statements that have reached the people through the press of the great economies the minister is effecting, all of which were due to the continuing of the ascending scale rate that we put into effect. I would not like to see the minister robbed of the benefit of that just as the time of fruition is arriving. I would like to see him get the benefit of the better showing which our legislation might bring forth. Why should he want to deny himself now? Would he not have been better to stand to his guns and be, at least, in a position to show the result of the legislation of others?

May I say, in brief, that the argument which my right hon. friend has just placed before the House from different standpoints, is incorrect from each standpoint? As regards what he said last, that the increase-
The better showing.

-the " better showing " was due to an act passed in 1920, that is not the fact. May I take the House into confidence for a moment, and say that when I came into office, I found that an order in council had been passed by the administration of which my right hon. friend was a member, taking away from the Postmaster General the right to make railway mail rates and vesting that power in the Board of Railway Commissioners? That was obviously done to make a better showing for the Canadian National railways, and it was of course acquiesced in by the other railways. I went to the trouble of taking a staff of officers to New York to investigate railway mail rates inasmuch as the order in council passed here was professedly based on American practice. After a week's intensive investigation in New York, I discovered, with the aid of my officials, that the Post Office Department was paying the railways of Canada as much to carry one mail bag in a baggage car, as the same railways charged to carry two passengers with their bags in a parlour car. Naturally, being a business man, I was not quite so innocent as to let that sort of thing continue. I had the order in council repealed and a new scale of railway mail rates adopted, as a result of which at one stroke we saved $400,000. In addition, I found that a considerable number of accounts for the carriage of mails of foreign countries across Canadian territory had not been attended to, nor had settlements been made. Settlements were negotiated, and eventually we succeeded in getting all those accounts settled, with the result that the treasury of the Dominion of Canada benefited to the extent of $950,000.
As a result of the International Postal Conference that was held last fall-and by the way it may surprise the committee to know that the work of that conference was concreted into a treaty which I signed, without any ambassador, British or American, intervening, acting solely under the powers conferred upon me as Canadian Postmaster General by the Canada Post Office Act-we saved at one stroke $110,000 which we formerly paid for the carriage of American mail across our territory from Buffalo to Detroit. Under the provisions of the treaty that we made last December the Americans agreed to relieve us of that payment. A further change that was made in consequence of the conference, was that we get from the United States payment on the excess parcels carried to Canada, an amount that will aggregate about $300,000 per annum. These are some of the new sources of revenue of the Post Office Department, without my going into the question of these rates at all.
As to the other argument of my right hon. friend that it is the small paper that is really affected, representations made to me are entirely contrary to that. The small papers are the papers that have pressed for this deduction. Only this morning I was informed by a gentleman engaged in the publication of a weekly newspaper, who is a very ardent supporter of my right hon. friend, that it is the

small papers that will be benefited, because they are the ones that are most affected.
The other argument that my right hon. friend used-that the daily papers would invade particularly the field of the local papers -is not a fact, because the big newspapers do not, as a matter of fact, use the post office for transmission within short distances. They send their papers by express. In the act, there is a section with which my right hon. friend was not familiar, which provides that papers issued not more than once a week are carried free of postage within an area of forty miles.
