I have only the details
mentioned. I think it is $1,300,000.

Then, as to the weeklies, there were only 20,000,000 pounds of weekly newspapers carried with a postage of $40,000. The net result would be that the rate at that [time amounted to $200,000 roughly speaking, which has been increased to $1,300,000.

The quarter-cent rate
prevailed at that time. It amounted to $290,000.

The memorandum goes on as follows:
No other country has as low a postage rate for newspapers as Canada. In fact, in every other country in the world, except Canada and the United States, postage on newspapers is prepaid by stamp affixed to each copy, [n many cases the rates go from 3 to 7 cents per pound. The rate is really more than this when it is considered that it is not a bulk rate but that each paper must bear its own postage, so that advantage cannot be taken of fractions as is the case in Canada and the United States where the rates are on the bulk weight of the mailings.
I would ask my hon. friend if that same condition applies to-day.

I would expect it would,
but I have not definite information.
I am so informed.
So, although the American rates were higher than ours they have been increased to a still greater sum.
I think the rates mentioned by my hon. friend are the rates in force at the present time.

That would be an increase from a minimum of two cents to a maximum of ten cents a pound according to the distance. In Great Britain the rate is a flat one of one cent per copy, which means a rate of at least three or four cents per pound on the bulk weight. Is that correct to-day?
I have no information as to that.

Again, am I right in this, that there was practically no increase made in so far as the rural weekly newspapers throughout the country are concerned, as a large part of their circulation is carried postage free. Does my hon. friend propose to disturb those conditions?

There was an exception
made for papers published not more than once a week. The weeklies were carried free within a radius of forty miles.

.Quite right,
could my hon. friend give me any other reasons for the adoption of the act other than those already given?

I do not know that I can add anything to the reasons already given. The representations made have been made, as I explained to the committee, at the instance largely of the smaller newspapers, the weekly papers, religious papers, technical papers, trade papers and other publications of that character.

It will be noticed from the figures supplied by the department itself, then, that it is the small end that is interested. The large end, the eighty per cent, are not interested in it at all. It used to be otherwise in days gone by. The big people, the eighty per cent, were the interested people and they thought they were paying a great deal too much and that we were doing a great deal for the small people in leaving
them as they were left. What I am doing now is merely showing justification for the action taken by the former government. I am not now going to oppose what my hon. friend is doing. I know it is no good, but I think we have to show a complete justification for our course, Mr. Chairman, when on the admitted figures the revenues then obtained were $290,000 and the cost of carrying the service was over $4,900,000. The revenue to-day is bettered being $1,300,000 as stated by my hon. friend, but the cost apparently remains constant with the exception of sixty per cent of $400,000, or $240,000. Of course, my hon. friend does not dispute the original figures. What is my hon. friend's estimate as to the reduction in revenue when this change is made?

The estimated reduction
will be about $200,000 on the $1,300,000. I would draw attention to the fact that the special committee of the cabinet, of which my hon. friend was a member, had before it all this data and with that data before it it decided not to impose a higher maximum rate, than l\ cents.
I take it that my hon. friend agrees that we went far enough.
It has been claimed you went too far.

My hon. friend evidently thinks we went far enough. Although the deficits were great we did not take it all up, I admit that. Has my hon. friend any figures in connection with the supplementary estimates that are brought down?
The Post Office has complied strictly with the request of the Minister of Finance to practise economy and has brought down no supplementary estimates.

I am very glad to hear that, and yet I am sorry, because I wanted to discuss a matter with the minister. I was going to ask him when the orders and the recommendations of the Civil Service Commission are going to be given effect to in his department.

The orders and recommendations of the Civil Service Commission have been given effect to as rapidly as possible, and if there are any still remaining for attention they will receive my attention as soon as the House prorogues.

I am very glad to have that assurance from my hon. friend, because it has seemed to be years before we could get any action out of the department.
Post Office Act

The weather is warm and molasses ought to move freely now but in this case the molasses seems to be frozen all the time. There are appointments dating back for many months. If the minister looks into the matter he will find there was a list given to the House, but the Acting Postmaster General could not do anything about it in the absence of the head of the department. I do hope that something will be done now. I merely want to point out to my hon. friend that, so far as I have been able to ascertain, the period of time allowed in connection with temporary appointees is long since passed and that the payments made to them are entirely illegal.

I almost hesitate to intervene in the dialogue between the Postmaster General (Mr. Murphy) and the ex-Minister of Finance (Sir Henry Drayton), but I should like to say a word in connection with the rate on newspapers. I do not think the rate affects dailies as much as some would suppose, but it is a matter of concern to quite a few very important weekly newspapers that circulate all over the Dominion. I must say that it benefits our people to a very large extent to be furnished with these papers at a reasonable rate. In the case of these weeklies I should think the increase in the rate per pound would affect them very seriously. For that reason I should almost be inclined to reduce the rate to one cent instead of one and a quarter cents. However, since the exMinister of Finance is pleased with it I think we might, perhaps, let the proposed rate go through.
I did not express any such opinion.

I do not know whether this is the proper time to register a protest against the increasing size of the newspapers of today. I think they are becoming almost a nuisance on that account. It may be deemed presumptuous on my part to indulge in anything like criticism along this line, but it does seem pertinent when we hear the talk about the increasing cost of paper and other expenses in connection with the production of newspapers. I suppose the increased size of our daily journals is to be attributed to the volume of advertising. I sometimes pick up a newspaper and notice that it is entirely blank except for some such announcement as this: "This space is reserved. Watch out for to-morrow." I think that in the matter of size our newspapers are almost getting beyond the limit, and if this policy continues I should almost be inclined to add a little more to the postage rate.
fSir Henry Drayton.]
There is another thing to which I desire to refer. I do not want to waste time but I should like to take this opportunity of making this statement. I hope I am not lacking in a sense of humour, but I do not always like the funny page in our newspapers. I do protest against pages that are supposed to be funny but in reality are not so.
Do not cut out "Mutt and Jeff."

Of course, other people may view this matter in a different light. I am pleased to see this reduction in the rate on newspapers. I think it will be of advantage to people living in rural communities. Living in this city, as I have been for the past five months, I appreciate the privilege city people have of getting the newspaper handed in to them at their door every morning, and I am prepared to encourage as much as possible anything that will promote the circulation of newspapers in the rural districts.

I should like to ask the minister a question but first I will say for the benefit of the hon. member for Brandon (Mr. Forke) that probably the managers of some of the large newspapers in this country had better send for him so that he may tell them how to run their journals.
Thank you, you are very kind.

It reminds me of the statement made by some hon. gentlemen to my left that a great many people are telling the farmers how to farm. In this case the hon. member for Brandon is telling the newspapers how to conduct their business.
Excuse me. I did not speak about the production of newspapers, I spoke from the viewpoint of the reader.

It did not strike me that way. The Postmaster General was good enough to say to the ex-Minister of Finance that immediately after prorogation he would attend to cases where certificates of appointment have been given postmasters, and other officials of the department, by the Civil Service Commission, but had not been acted on. During the Postmaster General's absence we had a short discussion here on the appointment of a postmaster at Clementsport, Nova Scotia. speakeroldname: Hon. CHARLES STEWART (Argenteuil) (Minister of Immigration and Colonization):
speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
moved the second reading of and concurrence in the amendments made by the Senate to Bill No. 45, an Act respecting Chinese Immigration.
He said: I do not wish to concur in all the amendments without discussion.
The usual move is for the House to receive the senate amendments and deal with them in the regular procedure, but a part of that procedure is a full explanation to the House.
The hon. member might explain the nature of the amendments, and then the question could be put.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
The senate has amended paragraph n of section 8. That paragraph reads:
(n) Persons over fifteen years of age, physically capable of reading, who cannot read the English or the French language or some other language or dialect. For the purpose of ascertaining whether aliens can read, the immigration officer shall use slips of uniform size pre-

pared by direction of the minister, each containing not less than thirty and not more than forty words in ordinary use printed in plainly legible type in the language or dialect the person may designate as the one in which he desires the examination to be made, and he shall be required to read the words printed on the slip in such language or dialect. The provisions of this paragraph shall not apply to Canadian citizens, or to persons in transit through Canada;
They have struck out the words-
The provisions of this paragraph shall not apply to Canadian citizens or to persons in transit through Canada;
And they have substituted:
The provisions of this paragraph shall not apply to persons residing in Canada at the date of the passing of this act, nor to Canadian citizens.
I may say for the information of the House that evidently the intent of the Senate was that it should not apply to Chinese now resident in Canada. I have no serious objection to offer to this, because in cases where the question of deportation of Chinese nationals who are in Canada might come up, we would not be likely to utilize this method of deporting.
Then clause 10 reads:
10. (1) The controller shall have authority to determine whether an immigrant, passenger or other person seeking to enter or land in Canada or detained for any cause under this Act is of Chinese origin or descent and whether such immigrant, passenger or other person, if found to be of Chinese origin or descent, shall be allowed to enter, land or remain in Canada or shall be rejected and deported.
(2) The examination of persons of Chinese origin or descent applying for admission or entry to Canada shall be separate and apart from the public and in the presence of such persons only as the controller shall permit.
They have added to that this clause:
Provided that if, on the preliminary hearing, the controller is not satisfied that such person is entitled to remain in Canada, the hearing shall be thereupon adjourned for forty-eight hours or for such longer period as the controller may see fit, and an opportunity shall be given such person to consult with duly accredited legal counsel who shall be entitled to represent him upon the hearing and upon all subsequent proceedings.
What it means is that when a decision that involves deportation is arrived at by the controller, a further hearing is guaranteed the applicant after the period of forty eight hours to permit him to secure counsel. I do not know that one should object to that particularly.
An amendment is made by the Senate to clause 18. The clause reads:
Within 12 months after the coming into force of this act and subject to such regulations as may be made by the Governor General in Council for the purpose, every person of Chinese origin or descent in Canada, irrespective of allegiance or citizenship, shall register with such officer or officers and at such place

Chinese Immigration Act
or places as are designated by the Governor General in Council for that purpose, and obtain a certificate in the form prescribed.
The amendment is to insert the following:
Provided that those persons who may, during the time fixed for registration, be absent from Canada with authority to return, may register upon their return.
It will be somewhat embarrassing to registration officials to work this out, because it will have to be done at a designated time and over a designated period. If a resident of Canada is absent on permit and does not return within the specified time when the registration is going on, this is evidently for the purpose of allowing him to become registered or to make application for registration.
Does not the bill as introduced by the minister provide that when an oriental leaves this country and goes to his home, he may not return?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
No. He
gets a permit upon which he may be absent for a specified time, and upon his return he presents that certificate.
Clause 26 has been amended. When the bill was in committee, one important amendment to clause 26 was submitted by the hon. member for Comox-Albemi (Mr. Neill). The clause as passed by this House reads:
Whenever any officer or peace officer has reason to believe that any person of Chinese origin or descent has entered or remains in Canada-
The amendment of my hon. friend added to the officers who would have authority to demand the production of a certificate or to make an explanation of any who were thought to be in Canada illegally. Instead of this being confined to officers of the department, peace officers of the government were included. The Senate amendment is to strike out the words "or peace officer."
Does the minister approve that? If he does, I should like to say a word in regard to it, but if not,-

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: That is my understanding.

Presumably the Senate were
animated by some reason or motive. Did they hint at or give any explanation of what that reason was?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I think representations were made to the Senate by people acting on behalf of the Chinese that this was rather drastic, and they thought, perhaps, it was too drastic to include the whole police force in this particular work. As I pointed out to my hon. friend from Vancouver Centre (Mr. Stevens), there may be some virtue in making selections of various persons throughout the country to do this particular work.
Further down, the same clause 26 reads:
The officer may detain such person in custody and bring him before the nearest controller for examination, and if the controller finds that he has entered or remains in Canada contrary to the provisions of this act or the Chinese Immigration Act or any amendment thereof, such person shall be deported.
The Senate have substituted the word "'may" for the word "shall." We had some discussion upon the meaning of that particular word when we were discussing the bill in committee, but I do not believe this amendment makes much difference. It is in the discretion of the minister or the controller how he shall act in that particular case.
Clause 27 of the bill is struck out entirely and a new clause substituted. The new clause reads:
27. (1) Every person of Chinese origin or descent resident in Canada at the date of the coming into force of this act, who was admitted under the provisions of any act now or heretofore in force, and did not secure such admission by fraudulent misrepresentation, and does not belong to any of the prohibited classes of persons described in section 8 of this act, shall be deemed to be entitled to continue to reside in Canada: Provided, however, that any such person who was. subsequent to the 25th day of July, 1917, admitted without payment of the head tax because of his being a merchant and who has ceased to belong to such class, shall pay into the Consolidated Revenue Fund of Canada the sum of five hundred dollars, and if he refuses or fails to make such payment he shall ipso facto forfeit his right to remain in Canada, and may be arrested by any officer without a warrant and brought before a controller for examination, whereupon he shall be dealt with to all intents and purposes in the same manner and subject to the same provisions as in the case of a person apprehended under section 26 of this act.
(2) Any person admitted under this act who at any time after admission ceases to belong to any of the classes admissible under this Act shall, unless he is a Canadian citizen, ipso facto forfeit his right to remain in Canada and may be arrested by any officer without a warrant and brought before a controller for examination, whereupon he shall be dealt with to all intents and purposes in the same manner and subject to the same provisions as in the case of a person apprehended under section 26 of this act.
Chinese Immigration Act

It was not the intention of the department to do anything more than is contained in this amendment. That is, it was not the intention of the department to disturb any Chinese national who was in Canada legally at the time of the registration, because this refers to the registration. The intention
4 p.m. was to deal only with those who were illegally in Canada at that time. It is alleged that in 1920 a very considerable number including many labourers, came in under a section permitting merchants to enter Canada. This amendment makes it a little difficult to deal with a labourer who came in two years ago as a merchant, but has been engaged in manual labour since, a3 it gives him the choice of paying the $500 head tax or being deported. In dealing with the nationals of any country who are admitted by making false representations, we have not very much leeway. The natural course would be to deport them. Probably not more than thirteen or fourteen hundred persons would be affected by this amendment.
Who would be the judge of whether a man is a merchant or a labourer?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
It is alleged that a number of these men never were merchants, and came in by misrepresentation. However, Mr. Speaker, rather than lose the effect of the balance of the legislation which we think it is in the interests of the department to have, I move that we accept the Senate amendment.

House again in committee on bill No. 238 to amend the Feeding Stuffs Act, Mr. Gordon in the chair.
On section 1-Definition. Bran, pure shorts, etc.
Has the minister any explanation to give the committee regarding the proposed changes in the bill?

The committee will recall that this matter was pretty fully discussed under the resolution, which was changed to a certain extent. Since then the millers' representatives have discussed the bill with some of the members of the Advisory Board under the Seed Control Act, who informed me that the agreement arrived at between the millers, the live stock men and the produce dealers is, in their estimation, the fairest

arrangement that can be devised. I pointed out to them that this House has the last word in respect to these matters, and that the consensus of opinion seemed to be in favour of keeping each mill by-product distinct. The millers' representatives pointed out that if this were done the millers would once more have to change their appliances, having already changed them to comply with the recommendations of the Advisory Board in such a way as to have four of the by-products pure, with a fifth consisting of a mixture of screenings and shorts. I have looked into the matter pretty carefully and I think that if we get four by-products of the mill in their purity it will be in the interests of buyers to allow a mixed feed of screenings and shorts, for which there must be a demand or the mills would not make it. Primarily the demand for this mixture must come from those who use it, mostly farmers. Naturally the millers want to meet that detnand.
i
Has the department full knowledge that the millers could not buy screenings at Fort William for shipment to their mills, there to be ground and mixed with shorts?
That is quite right, the millers could do so. But as far as I can make out screenings are not sufficiently popular down here for the millers to do so.
Is the minister satisfied that the demand by farmers for mixed feed is sufficient to justify the mixture?

What else would induce the millers to manufacture it? I am trying to be fair to all sides. As far as I understand the situation, while the millers may defeat the purpose of the bill, it seems to me it is in their interests not to do so, because they must please their customers with this mixture. They have four by-products in their purity-bran, shorts, middlings and low grade flour, and it is at the option of the buyer to ask for a mixture of screenings and shorts. Really, in our own interests as farmers I do not think we should be so exacting in our determination to have all these byproducts in such an absolute condition of purity. You cannot get the best-balanced ration of fodder without a mixture. I am not a miller, fc>ut I am placing the arguments of the millers before hon. members. They take this ground: If you do not permit us to mix anything with the screenings to make them more acceptable to the buyer, we have to lose money by selling the screenings unmixed.
I understand that they are quite unpopular down here.

Feeding Stuffs Act
Hear, hear.
Not because they are bad feed.
Yes, there is nothing else in it but screenings.

The term "mill
screenings" suggests refuse, more or less. I have bought mill screenings at the Saskatoon elevator that were as good a hog feed as I ever fed. I do not understand the prejudice against it down here, but it does seem to exist. If they have to dispose of these screenings without being permitted to mix them with anything to make them more acceptable, there will have to be a loss and I suppose they will have to make it up on something else. I do not know whether there is anything in that or not, but I am placing the matter before the committee. We want to do what is in the interests of both parties concerned, the mills and the buyers of mill products.

I understand
that when the wheat is bought by the miller it is bought with a certain dockage; the screenings are the result of the dockage and cost the miller practically nothing. It should be insisted upon that an analysis of these different foods be set out on the label attached to each sack. I have in mind the situation that existed during the war where the millers in Ontario reground bran and sold it to the farmers as shorts. Had an analysis of that material been furnished, it would clearly have been shown to be bran, but as it was, the persons who bought it were deceived; they not only paid a higher price but they paid for something they did not really get. There has been a lot of deception in the case of mill feeds and I think we should provide every possible safeguard. I am against anything being done to allow the millers to mix feeds unless they will state on the tags exactly what the analysis of the mixture is. That is a necessary safeguard to the buyers of the product.
That is fair enough. The bill provides exactly for that.
Not the analysis.
Yes, the analysis is here; the exact fibre content is shown. If the bran is ground into shorts, that will be known, because the fibre content will be stated.
It will not state the amount of protein, carbohydrates and fat.

No, you will have to go into that further. But the fibre content is an indication of whether the material is bran or shorts or whether one has been converted into the other. As to the cost, my experience has been that wheat stored in the terminals, from which the millers usually buy, is purchased out of the terminals and paid for on its gross weight. When it is inspected at Winnipeg the inspection certificate will state not only the grade but also the dockage, if any. When it is sent to Fort William the inspectors must see thaut when it is unloaded it is put into its proper grade, and the proper amount of cleaning is done to make it come up to the inspection certificate. When that is done and it is warehoused it is bought as wheat and paid for as wheat. That is my understanding of it, and I have reasonable knowledge of the conditions. What other system could you have? When that wheat goes into the Fort William or any other terminal elevator and is commercially cleaned, it still contains so much screenings that it cannot be ground out that way. You have to go further than having it commercially cleaned; as a miller you have to clean it yourself and take out certain commodities in the way of refuse. It is permissible for this stuff to go into the general bin and even to go over for export, but it has to be taken out by whatever miller uses the wheat. Yet it is paid for as wheat. Well, what are you going to do with it? It is really a mill by-product; it is what was grown by and bought from the farmers. The contention is that if a mixture is produced of these screenings and short3 and they are labelled accordingly, there will be no deception.
What I want to get at is the best possible way of dealing with this question that has been on the boards now for quite a while. I am afraid that the milling industry ran a little loose some years ago in the unauthorized mixing of screenings. Legislation was later brought in under which they were authorized to do general mixing, and you could hardly get a better brand of shorts which has none of these mill screenings in it. There is still the suggestion that a compounding of mill screenings and shorts be permitted. If the committee do not want that; if they think it is not in the interests of anybody, particularly of the buyer, let us have it out, but let us not, out of prejudice to the mill, hurt those who have to buy this product. I assume that the reason why the mills want to make it that way is because somebody wants to buy it that way.
Feeding Stuffs Act
But the buyers cannot get anything else. They have to take the adulterated stuff; they have no option in the matter.
Oh, they have the option.
It is not available; the mills do not manufacture it.

The minister laid emphasis on the fact that the millers buy wheat and pay for it as wheat, notwithstanding the fact that there is a certain proportion of screenings in it. That is true, of course, in regard to the wheat actually going through the terminals at Fort William. But how about the mills situated all through western Canada which buy wheat from the threshing machines, which buy large quantities of screenings that they do not pay for? In that case they get the stuff absolutely free. I saw something in one of the mills last fall that made me feel pretty strongly on this point.
I saw not only screenings, but scourings, dirt, sweepings, going into the shorts, and when I remembered that that shorts was on occasions used for human food, I felt disgusted. It is unfortunate that we should have to make regulations governing the mills in the interests of the consumer, but I do not see how we can do anything else. These mills are equipped with the very best machinery to take out every grain of wild oats, every one of the smallest seeds. The wheat is ground absolutely pure, so that the flour is pure, the bran and shorts are pure. Now, are we to allow them to go back and mix in all kinds of rubbish? It may be said that the miller should be allowed to do what he pleases with his own product. But this stuff is palmed off on a helpless public, who, in the great majority of cases have no opportunity of knowing what they are buying, who are compelled to buy this stuff because they cannot get a pure product. I do not think we should countenance any other law than that these products should be kept absolutely pure. I am aware that many of our western screenings have good feeding value, such as wild oats, wild buckwheat, and that some of the screenings are made up of cracked and broken wheat, which has a large feed value. But there are years when our western crops contain large quantities of seeds that are of little or no value compared with these. Very often we have large quantities of pigweed seed, French weed, mustard and other weeds.' These things are all ground up and put into the bran and shorts, and sometimes the bran and shorts are left in such a way that
I Mr. Motherwell.]
they are so unpalatable to the stock that they will not take them, and the man who has bought them has no redress. The minister knows this as well as the rest of us from the West. We do not need to convince him personally that the interests of the public are jeopardized so long as this mixing of screenings with good wholesome bran and shorts goes on. If it continues to go on, probably pure bran and shorts will be on the market in such limited quantities that it will not be possible for us to get them at all.

Does the minister
know that the millers in the province of Ontario mix with the bran and shorts the dust and dust screenings from oatmeal? I know that hundreds of tons of these dust screenings are mixed in with other feed in the province of Ontario. I am strongly opposed to anything being mixed with these screenings.

There are two
sides to the question. There have been abuses with regard to mixing feeds in the past, and the point is, shall we go from the one extreme of allowing indiscriminate mixing to the other extreme of not allowing any mixing at all? That is the alternative. Is there not a middle course of having a mixture for the buyer who wants to buy mixed feed? If there is I would suggest to every member of the committee that, after we are through discussing it, we have a vote regardless of where we are sitting, just on the merits of the question, and see if we cannot come to a decision. If we do that nobody can have any grievance; I am sure I will not have. I think that is the best course to take in regard to the matter because it seems to me unwise to rush from the one extreme of indiscriminate mixing to the other extreme of not allowing any mixing at all. I have indicated to the millers' representatives that if one mixture is allowed, that is the mixture of screenings and shorts, and they do not play fair with it in the next year, I shall be one of the very first to cut this mixing down to a minimum. We are giving them that advantage not in their interests alone but in the interests of the buyers of these feeds.

May I
suggest to the minister that the mixing can always be done, and it is done to a large extent to-day, by the producer of the stock. If I want a mixed feed I can buy the feeds and mix them myself. I much prefer mixing my own feeds to having them mixed by someone I do not know anything about.

It is not often
done.
It will be done.

I was not in when this discussion started and I am surprised at the trend of it now because I thought this matter was1 all settled on June 22 when the bill was up for second reading. I am sympathetically that way yet.

One of the reasons the bill is before my hon. friend in the form it is, is that it was reprinted in accordance with the amended resolution, but unfortunately one page of it was left exactly the way it was, while the other was according to the resolution. We had to take something, so we took the original bill.

The minister seems to
have very bad luck in having his bills printed. Pei'haps we should get a special proof-reader for his bills. But the minister's explanation is no excuse for going back on the amendment that was adopted the other evening, and I would suggest to him that if we do not make the corrections in committee here now, he had better withdraw the bill and have it reprinted.
The minister suggests that we take a vote. We cannot take a vote in committee unless there is a motion made to amend the bill or on a motion that the committee rise or a clause be passed.

We have not yet
reached the stage of making a motion.
Would the minister permit the committee to discuss the motion before we vote on it? If he is going to have a motion let us have it.

Perhaps the committee will allow me to make a few remarks on this question. As chairman of the committee on Agriculture and Colonization, I was present as a member of the advisory council which met here in the winter. On that council were representatives of the feeders, the breeders, the millers-

What were their
names?
I have not a list of the names here.
We would like to have them.
The department would have the list.
Who appointed this committee?
It was appointed, I think, by the department or by the Seed branch.

I forget the names of the members. They were from western Ontario. I think one of them was Mr. Breth-our. Two of the millers were Mr. Cornell and Mr. G. B. Watts, of Toronto. There were twelve or fifteen representatives altogether, and I had met only two or three of them before. All interests were represented on that council. My hon. friend should not shake his head. It is a regular thing to have advisory boards of this character. There are advisory boards in connection with half of the acts we pass. He must not be disappointed if I cannot remember all the names.
Is it not on the recommendation of the minister that this board is appointed? He names the members of the board.

No, the live stock associations select their own representatives, the produce men and the millers theirs. The department has one or two representatives on the board including Mr. Clark of the Seed branch, but the others are appointed by the different interests.

Section 14 of the act clearly provides that the minister shall have power to appoint an advisory board who will at his request prepare and recommend to him such regulations as appear to them advisable to make under this act. This is the authority of the minister to appoint this advisory council.
Feeding Stuffs Act
We will do the formal appointing, I have no doubt, on the recommendations given to us by these respective bodies.

In view of the fact that there are seven pages of regulations in connection with the act made on the recommendations of this board, I think it is proper that the committee should know the status of this board and the names of those who were present considering this matter.
Who were the live stock men?

I remember that Mr. Stonehouse was there, representing the Eastern Dairymens' Association; Mr. Brethour representing the Swine Breeders' Association, and two or three other members representing live stock associations. I was appointed to represent the committee on Agriculture on that board. Dr. Grisdale was also there, Dr. Shutt, Mr. Archibald, Mr. White, all of the Department of Agriculture; and Mr. Clark, the Seed Commissioner, was the chairman. After three days' discussion on the various matters relating to live stock industry, on feeds and other questions of interest to the breeders, a day was spent in discussing bran, shorts, and middlings. This bill practically represents the conclusions which were arrived at at that meeting. The live stock men there felt that it was most desirable that all the mill feeds- bran, shorts, middlings and feeding flour-should be absolutely pure. That is the aim which all the live stock men hope to attain ultimately. But during the conference the point of view of the millers was advanced. And we came to the conclusion that under the present conditions-so long as the farmers will grow weeds and produce weed seeds and screenings, and in view of the fact that the millers buy these screenings and must dispose of them after having bought them-the best interests of the live stock men would be served by having bran, middlings, and feed flour always pure, but allowing the screening, to a certain extent, to be mixed with the shorts. Feeders will remember that for many years screenings have been mixed with shorts, bran and feed flour, and it was with the object of having the screenings in one place and one place only that this agreement was arrived at
The hon. member for North Ontario (Mr. Halbert) asked the minister, if the mills could buy screenings as such by the car load, and bring them in and mix them up with their shorts. I understand that Mr. Clark, of the Seed branch, and the department know or can
I Mr. Sutherland.]
ascertain where every car load of screenings goes which leaves Fort William. Now, it is no doubt true that the mills who buy from the interior elevators buy their wheat subject to dockage-
You say the department know where every load of screenings goes? Knowing that why can they not prohibit the millers from grinding screenings and mixing them with shorts?

The department are enabled to ascertain whether the millers are doing this or not. If the millers buy any quantities of screenings separately from the wheat, the officials of the department know that and steps can be taken to prevent their buying screenings in order to mix them with shorts.. As far as the wheat bought from the elevators at Fort William is concerned I understand it contains a certain percentage of weed seeds or screenings up to about three per cent. Those screenings the millers pay for as wheat and wish to incorporate in the shorts. Now if there is not more than three per cent of screenings from the wheat which the millers buy and that is mixed with the shorts, I do not think the farmers will suffer to any great extent, because it was brought out at that meeting by many of the breeders that they desired to buy screenings as they were valuable for food. The chemical analysis given by Dr. Shutt of the value of screenings is very high, showing that they are worth more as a feed than shorts. Farmers well know that you cannot use screenings, however, for feeding young animals. If young pigs, for example, are fed with screenings to any extent it will cause indigestion and very often death.
I have seen screenings mixed with shorts and hogs refused to eat it. Other farmers have seen the same thing happen.
Of course, screenings should not be fed to young pigs or young calves, but they appear to be an excellent food for mature stock.

You say the department knows where every car load of screenings goes. Now, suppose the department finds that a miller is buying screenings and mixing them with shorts, is there no way of penalizing the miller for doing so? What procedure does the department take in such a case?
In the past it has been legal for them to do so.

But will it be under the bill as now proposed?

Feeding Stuffs Act

I do not think there is anything in this bill to prevent it. But the minister says that if the millers are found to be buying screenings and mixing them up with their feeds he will bring down legislation to prevent it another year. I do not think the millers could do that to any great extent without being found out.

Do you think the millers would undergo any hardship in being compelled to grind screenings separately and selling them for what they are? My impression is that if you allow this privilege to the millers of mixing feeds we are going to have feeds foisted on the purchaser that are not of the character he thinks they are.
I think there can be no hardship, none at any rate that I can see, in saying to the miller "You grind your shorts separately and sell it as shorts, grind your screenings and shorts separately." The purchaser can mix them if he wants to.

To hark back to this advisory council. I am quite frank in saying that my own desire, and the desire of the breeders and the department officials who were present at the conference, was to have all the mill offal from wheat absolutely pure. I make no bones about that. I look forward to the day when that will be brought about.
Why not now?

I will explain why the advisory council came to the decision they did. The millers have their point of view. They pointed out that they were paying for these screenings and were entitled to sell them. They pointed out that if they were compelled to keep the screenings separate and not mix them with one of the three by-products it would entail very heavy expense in changing the machinery of the mill. It would mean that every miller would have to add another conveyor to his mill, in order to have the screenings separated from the other feed.

Why did the millers not wait till the bill went through before doing anything? They fixed the mill over before the bill went through, and now they want the matter arranged after we pass the act. Why did they not wait till the bill went through the committee? You say millers have changed their mills.

No, they would have to change them. If you do not allow screenings to be added to the three by-products, the millers will have to change their mills, and will have
to add another conveyor, in order to keep the screenings away from the mill feeds.

Is it not a fact that the screenings and shorts are now separate, and they have to have a conveyor to convey them together? Would it not simplify the matter to keep them separate when they are separate?

I am afraid I am not an expert on milling; I know very little about it. But the millers who appeared before this committee were able to convince the committee that they had a good case, and that was the argument they put up. The members of that committee were a pretty representative body of men. They had a desire for pure feed.

Just to make my question a little clearer, is it not a fact that the screenings are all separate in wheat before it is ground, and when the wheat is ground and the shorts separated from the bran and other mill feeds, they are all apart? They have to put in conveyors to convey their screenings into the shorts at the present time and mix them again.

Well, I have stated the argument that they put up. I am not going to undertake to go into the details of the milling business. I understand that it would entail a very heavy expenditure on each mill, if they were compelled to keep their screenings separate. I understand, there is a conveyor for bran, another for shorts and another for middlings-three conveyors. This is to convey the ground feed to the mixing room. They can take the screening.? and mix them with one of the three products, or mix them with all three, and use the machinery they have. That is the argument which they presented to this committee. If you compel the mills to add this expense and make the extra investment, the result will be that the cost of our feed will go up.

I would like the hon. member to show where the extra expense is; because certainly the waste is taken away from the wheat before it is ground. It is then reground and run back through the same spout as the other wheat.

If my hon. friends who are asking questions are experts on milling I would be glad if they will tell us the process of milling and grinding. I have said that I do not know. I only know what was stated before the advisory board. The arguments were advanced by the millers and feeders, and this bill represents the best judgment of that committee.
