Perhaps the hon. member would let the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Robb) tell us about the expense.
I think I had better finish my remarks, and the other members may then address the Chair.

Would the hon. member consider it more advisable to allow the millers to continue the present process by having some machinery in, rather than to discourage the breeding of live stock in this country? Which is the more important?

I do not quite get the gist of my hon. friend's remarks. I hope ultimately to have all the by-products of wheat pure; but I believe, and the members who were on this committee with me believed, that for the present the best interests of the farmers of this country and the interest of the breeders would be served by allowing the screenings to be mixed with the shorts.
May I ask a question?

I think I should be permitted
to finish and then I shall be pleased to answer questions later.

This is not a technical <juestion. I would like to ask the hon. member, just in what way did the committee consider it would benefit the breeders of live stock to have filth and screenings mixed with good feed?

There is a demand from many breeders for recleaned screenings. The millers said, "If you compel us to make all the byproducts of wheat pure, we will have to put up the price of the bran and shorts, feed-flour and middlings." It seemed to the majority of the members of that committee-and they were practically unanimous-that this was the best arrangement we could arrive at. That was the feeling after the meeting was over, because it was thought the screenings were a good thing. There is a certain demand for screenings, and screenings for the feeding of mature stock are a better food than shorts alone. So long as the farmer knows what he is buying,-so long as the container is marked "shorts" and "screenings," in letters the same size, or "pure shorts," or "pure bran," or "pure middlings" or "pure feed-flour," it was thought the farmers would be adequately protected against feeding screenings to young .stock, to which it would be injurious, as against compelling the mills to make it all pure. The reason was that we would get our *other feed at a cheaper price. That sums

up the argument as presented to us. I understand that the amount of recleaned screenings which left Fort William for the East last year was 12,000 tons, and 24,000 tons left the elevators to go West; and the total output of all the mills for the same year was 600,000 tons.
Of what?
The output of the mills of bran, shorts and feed-flour.
And flour too?
No.

If the mills would only
grind that recleaned screening there would not be any necessity for mixing it with anything else in order to have it sold at its feeding value. It is only because they want to mix in some of that dirt that has no feeding value that they want to cover it up in the bran and shorts. That is the plain situation- that our cleaned screenings are good feed, and no one will refuse to buy them at their value. We have seen them composed of a certain percentage of wild oats, cracked wheat and the flax and stuff that is real good, and will sell at their value anywhere; and it is only because the millers want to cover up the mustard and dirt and the wild unpalatable stuff that they put this in at all.

The weeds that go into the
large mills are very thoroughly cleaned. The mustard and the similar weeds are all taken out.
The contrary is absolutely the case.

I am nob talking about screenings which come from an elevator. I am talking about screenings which come from a mill after the wheat is cleaned ready for grinding. That is what goes into shorts at present. For the last year the mills, following this bill almost exactly, have been putting their screenings into their shorts, and they have been making bran middlings and feed-flour, clean.
On the advisory council, did these gentlemen mention anything about the point I brought up, about scourings being put in? I say that scourings are put in, and I know whereof I speak.

I agree with the hon. gentleman (Mr. Brown). The millers in the first place clean that wheat as thoroughly as

Feeding Stuffs Act
it is possible to clean it from all foreign substances. Now they want to pollute the by-products with mill sweepings and dirt of all kinds, and to make the mixture so that it is not fit for animal food. In my experience as a cattle breeder, I have come across instances where this was adulterated to such an extent that it was not fit for food at all. If they want to sell rubbish, let them sell it on its merits; if they want to sell screenings, let them sell that on its merits; but let them sell bran and shorts for what they really are as they come from the mill.
At the end of paragraph (d) clause 2, there are two lines which read:
No person shall manufacture pure shorts and shorts and mill screenings at the same mill.
What does that mean?
It was decided the other day to cut that out.

There is only one way by which we will get all our feeds pure, and that is when our friends in the West will have their grain cleaned as it leaves the elevators and will keep their dirt, weeds, and so forth, on their own farms.
That is our business.

What does the hon. member think of Ontario where we feed hundreds of thousands of tons of that stuff that comes east? How are we going to keep our farms in Ontario clean? No mill can grind all that stuff so as to kill all the weeds. We on this side of the House would like to know who on that committee were real farmers. I am afraid on that .committee there were only one or two men belonging to the farming industry. The rest were millers and sympathizers with the millers.
I do not think my hon. friend should make that statement. Why make a reflection-
It is no reflection.
-of that nature, when there is no justification for it?
He is not making a reflection.
The hon. gentleman pointed out that, with the exception of two men, the rest were sympathizers with the millers.
All right.
I was at a luncheon with them. Am I to be classified as a sympathizer with the millers?
Perhaps.

My hon. friend
may take that attitude if he likes. I said that I did not believe in going to the one extreme of mixing things indiscriminately, or to the other extreme of prohibiting mixing altogether.
Let us do the mixing ourselves.

If my hon. friend
knew a little more about the matter, he would know that that was not practicable. As regards what the hon. member for Lisgar (Mr. Brown) says, if these mills all bought their wheat directly from the farmers, he is absolutely right that they could do what they liked with the screenings; that they could 5 p.m. throw it into the gutter if they liked. It did not cost them anything except for handling. I do not know what percentage of wheat is marketed in that way, but a comparatively small quantity is purchased directly from the farmers, when one considers that our wheat is spread over the Dominion from the Atlantic to the Pacific. Let us forget the millers and think of those who are using those by-products. What is in their best interest? I am confident, if a waste ensues as a result of millers buying these screenings as wheat and not being able to sell it to advantage, or if a loss ensues thereby to the millers, they are bound to make that up by larger profits on some other branch of their activities. This is not like farming. If a farmer loses, he has to lose-I do not know how that comes about, but that is the way the thing works-if a manufacturer loses, he has some way of tacking that on to something else. You may think that is not right, but that is what happens. The miller i3 going to make more on his bran, shorts, middlings and low-grade flour, probably on his high-grade flour, to make up what he loses on the wheat. I am not arguing that that is right, but that is the way in which the thing works out. Is it in our interest to make a provision that results in that, and possibly to disappoint many farmers who want to buy that mixture? I see the hon. member for Glengarry and Stormont (Mr. Kennedy) having a good time listening. I do not suppose there is in this chamber an hon. gentleman who has more experience than he with regard to feeding by-products. I do not profess to
Feeding Stuffs Act

have such recent knowledge as he has, and I should like to hear what he has to say. My impression, as I say, is against any form of mixture. My judgment is that it is not wise to go to the other extreme and to prohibit it altogether. There are certain people who want to buy a blend. Why prevent them from buying it? There would be no deception. The fact that-it is a mixture will be marked on the bag. If you do not like to buy it, you lo not need to do so. You can take the pure stuff. You have the two choices, the mixture on the one hand, and the pure bran or shorts or middlings on the other. Let us forget that we have any sympathies or prejudices, and let us just use our judgment and get the best bill possible under the circumstances.
Would we have any way of knowing what quantity of shorts and screenings there were in the mixture? There might be a gallon of shorts and the rest screenings.
I know that is hard to regulate, but it is spoken of as "mill run.''
The minister says that there is no deception. Why not keep the screenings by themselves and let us do the mixing ourselves? Then there will be no deception.
If the committee is willing, I am agreeable.

I would like to give the hon. member for South Huron (Mr. Black) a list of the members on that committee. He stated that there were no members there representing the farmers. The chairman was Mr. Clark, Seed Commissioner of Canada. There was Dr. Grisdale, Deputy Minister of Agriculture, who could not be said to be in sympathy with the millers. Mr. J. E. Brethour, representing the Swine Breeders' Association of Ontario was a member. My hon. friend will know him as one of the best and biggest farmers in western Ontario. Mr. Stonehouse, of the National Dairy Council, was another member who was there representing the Eastern Dairymens' Association. The hon. member for Missisquoi (Mr. Kay) was a member, and he is a farmer of some repute. I do not think the hon. gentleman will doubt that statement. I happen to have had the privilege of being there myself. There were only three other gentlemen there representing the millers, as compared with six of us representing the farmers.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The debate is getting away from clause 1 which we are considering.

There seems to be a good
deal of discussion how bran, shorts and flour are manufactured. In my district there has been for the last thirty years, a mill to which we take wheat and get back flour, bran and shorts. Only those three products, nothing else, are manufactured at that mill. The wheat is certainly cleaned before it is ground, and the screenings are crushed and sold. These are the products: flour, bran, shorts, and the ground screenings can be purchased as chop which is good feed for either cattle or hogs. As regards the quantity, that miller would always give 36 pounds of flour, 10 of bran and 10 of shorts. There was thus 4 pounds left to take care of anything left in the wheat. They figured this a loss of four pounds on every bushel. Consequently the miller is suffering no loss at all. We know with certainty that the milling companies, having their elevators all over the three prairie provinces, are able to buy wheat extensively and it is docked as bought. The farmer is not paid for any screenings; these are made a present of to the miller and the freight is paid to Fort William. Besides, the millers are able to purchase wheat at the street price, that is, the Fort William price less storage and transportation charges; consequently if they ship those screenings out the freight is already paid. Therefore we who want pure bran and shorts demand the opportunity of getting them absolutely pure. Those of us last winter who wanted to buy pure bran could not get it, -there was 7 per cent of screenings in it. No mill in the country is so equipped as to be able to grind these screenings, they can be ground only at the big central mills. In a word, the mixture of screenings in our feed stuffs is a fraud, and we do not want to see it carried on any longer.

We are getting a
little light on this question of commercial feed stuffs. The minister (Mr. Motherwell) states that he is sympathetic with the desire to have all mill feeds pure, and the chairman of the committee on Agriculture (Mr. Kay) states that that is his view also, and that he hopes ultimately we will arrive at this desirable state of affairs. It seems to me that we are becoming a little more involved from year to year in dealing with this question. In 1919 the millers' representatives gave evidence before the committee on the Cost of Living, evidence which does not bear out the conclusions reached by the chairman of the committee on Agriculture. They claimed there was no difficulty whatever in keeping screenings separate, in fact it was stated that the

Feeding Stuffs Act
wheat had to go through seven different processes before it was in a condition fit to be milled into flour, and that the large mills contained up to date appliances by which the screenings could be ground and distributed equally among the by-products. It was claimed by the millers' representatives at that time that if they were not permitted to dispose of the screenings in this way they would have to increase the price of their flour. This was the excuse put forward. And in face of that we had abundance of evidence to show that thousands of animals were being poisoned as a result of this stuff being fed to them.

I do not think my hon. friend
wishes to misrepresent me. I do not say that the millers cannot separate the screenings from the other mill feed, but if they do separate them it will entail a heavy inves-ment on the part of each mill.

Mr. Black, of the
Ogdvie Milling Company, in his sworn evidence before the committee on June 23rd, 1919, was asked the question:
Nothing to do with the mills?
And he said in reply:
Nothing whatever. However, we could eliminate that if it was so desired, but we then would turn it over and sell it for what we could get. That might mean that you would have to increase the cost of the flour to some extent, because we might not be able to get as much for it in some other form as in brail or shorts.
They know very well they could not dispose of it as flour, but owing to the dark colour of the bran and shorts they could mix screenings and other dirt with it and in that way dispose of it. We had some very good evidence from the Minister of Agriculture and the member for Saltcoats (Mr. Sales) this session with regard to the methods pursued in the West. Apparently the latter has had practical experience, and so has the Minister of Agriculture. The member for Saltcoats was explaining how easy it was to take out most of these objectionable seeds right at the farm when the grain was being threshed. It is a very simple process. The thresher is paid so much per bushel but when there is a lot of weeds in the grain he stated that the farmer will not pay the thresher for the weed seeds if separated from the grain, consequently the thresher closes the shoe and allows all the weed seeds to come out with the grain, in this way getting paid for his threshing. "Everyone knows that," the minister called out across the House; "that is exactly what they do." Or words to that effect.
So we might as well look at this matter fairly and squarely. In fact the wheat purchased in western Canada that does not pass through the terminal elevators contains as much as 10 per cent weed seeds. Evidence before the committee showed that that is very often the case. Naturally, there is a great inducement for the millers to utilize this stuff in some way and dispose of it at a profit. I do not think there is any other way of dealing with this adulteration than by absolutely prohibiting millers mixing screenings with feed stuffs. Of course, they cannot possibly adulterate their flour in this way, but, so far as bran and shorts are concerned, the millers should not be permitted to put this dirt back into the bran and shorts.
Did the millers pay for the 10 per cent screenings in the wheat they purchased?

Not in the West. Where wheat is purchased at the elevators and cleaned and contains less than 3 per cent, the millers do pay; but not on grain purchased on the street and shipped direct without passing through the terminal elevator, unless they dock the seller of the grain. I do not know whether they do or not. In 1919 as a result of the evidence then obtained a bill was introduced by myself and referred to the committee on Agriculture for their consideration. The committee recommended that the bill should be put into effect. Thereupon the House passed the bill, which absolutely prohibited the adulteration of mill feeds such as bran and shorts in any way. The following session a Department of Health was created, and it took over part of the machinery for enforcing the act. I believe there is a fragment of this act on the statute books to-day. In the following session the present act was passed, and at the time I pointed out what I thought would be the result. I regret to say that exactly what I predicted has happened. I might be permitted to read one paragraph of my statement:
The effect of this clause will be that mill feeds of this kind will be mixed and you will get but a very small proportion of pure bran and shorts. This clause is a departure from the old act, end instead of being an advance along the lines which we desire, it is going in the opposite direction. It is making provision for the mixing of all these feeding stuffs and having the mixture disposed of to suit the convenience of the mill feed men.
What have we experienced since that time? We have found in Ontario-which I know better than any other part of the Dominion- that it is absolutely impossible to buy pure bran and shorts, although provision was made in the act for keeping those pure. But there is a distinction. These are sold as feed stuffs; the other is sold as commercial feed stuff, and
Feeding Stufis Act

must have printed on the container, "Screenings not exceeding mill run." You will find these words on the bottom of the container, but it gets covered over and no one realizes it is there. Under the present act a farmer is not often able to purchase pure mill feed, but has to take what he can get at the price demanded. This stuff is being palmed off on the farmers and their stock poisoned in consequence. The Department of Agriculture has abundant evidence to show that this is the case. This evidence has been put on record on previous occasions, and I shall not take up the time of the committee in referring to it. But the minister says he has intimate knowledge of the conditions both in western and in eastern Canada, and he says that his sympathies are with the keeping of mill feeds pure. He should, therefore, take steps to see that that is done. I wrote the minister a year ago in regard to the matter and was informed that some steps were to be taken to provide a remedy. I directed his attention to the subject on two or three occasions during the present session, and I was informed that a bill to this effect would be brought down. I have only to-day had an opportunity of looking over the bill;-I was not here when the resolution was discussed last week,-and I must say I am very much disappointed to find that there is to be no progress along the desired lines.
What is the use of trying to make the people believe that the millers cannot overcome the difficulties? The millers can adapt themselves to these conditions very quickly, if a change is demanded and if they do so they will find it much more satisfactory in the end; they will find that there will be a greater demand for mill feeds than there has ever been. The farmers are passing through a trying period. The one hope for the future of agriculture is the live stock industry, and you cannot successfully engage in that industry without an abundance of mill feeds such as bran and shorts. Under the old system of milling there were only the three products, but with the modern system there are four or five different products. By the way, this matter of an increase in products was referred to the committee on Agriculture two years ago and it was then decided that the sale of a new product of the milling of wheat would not be permitted. I was amazed to find that notwithstanding that attitude of the committee on Agriculture, the department did put this measure into effect. The recommendations of the committee were adsolutely ignored and the requests of the millers were granted. I am afraid the millers are the only ones who are receiving considera-
[ Mr. Sutherland.]
tion to-day. I regret very much to have to speak in this way, but I have taken a stand on this matter for the last ten years, and the conditions instead of getting better are getting worse from year to year. The farmers are getting discouraged. Buildings that have cost them hundreds, in some cases, thousands of dollars, are to-day empty. They are not engaging in the raising of hogs, a branch of farming that should be very profitable, to anything like the extent desirable. Now, something should be done. The minister does not appear to realize that this advisory committee was appointed on his recommendation.

The names were
recommended to me.

The member for
Muskoka (Mr. Hammell) has given us some information as to who they were; I believe there was authority for appointing about sixteen members on that committee. Now, we have had a special committee on Agriculture sitting from almost the beginning to the end of this session; they could have looked into this matter had it been referred to them, and I think they would have been better employed than they were, because apparently not much consideration was given to this question. Let me inform the committee as to something that happened in 1917. A very strenuous debate has taken place for several sessions with regard to the manufacture of oleomargarine. It is important to note that the first steps taken to destroy the commercial feed stuffs and the grain standards of this country were taken by order in council in December 1917 on the recommendation of the then Minister of Agriculture, the hon. member for Marquette (Mr. Crerar). I have copies of the orders in council here. Steps were taken also to purchase the screenings at the terminal elevators at S35 a ton, and for some time they were disposed of to the farmer. In view of the mixture which was permitted I have come to the conclusion-because the Oleomargarine Act was put through just about the same time-that the idea was to obtain a feed for a dairy cow with a view to producing oleomargarine instead of butter. There is an item in the supplementary estimates of $700,000 for the health of animals. I say that if you put something in this bill that will prevent the adulteration of mill feeds you will do more for the health of animals than the voting of this $700,000 to which I refer, or than the payment of $900,000 for veterinary and lay inspectors in the abattoirs and elsewhere throughout the country, as now provided for.

Feeding Stuffs Act

I do not wish to delay the committee very long, because several members have already referred to the extent of the practice of mixing foul seed with mill feed. For many years it has been most difficult to get bran that is fit to feed to thfc>
stock, in fact in many cases the stock turn from it. One hon. member has stated that if we do not enact the legislation now before us, it will be necessary for the mills, at considerable expense, to change their machinery. But I assure the committee that unless a change is made very soon it will be a case either of the mills changing their machinery or of some of the live stock changing their digestive apparatus. When foul seed, which are bitter in taste, are ground up and mixed with the bran the resulting mixture is not only unpalatable but injurious to the health of the animals. At first it appeared to me to be not unwise to allow this bill to go through, the Minister of Agriculture having said that the purchasers would have an opportunity of buying or of not buying, as they pleased; they could get the pure bran or they could get the mixture. On second thought, however, I do not think it would be wise to do that. There has been much abuse in the past, and in all probability very little of the pure bran would be offered for sale if this was permitted. The farmers who wanted feed very badly would be willing to pay a higher price for the pure feed if they could get it, but the pure feed not being available they would be forced to buy the impure stuff. I do not see any reason why any suggested necessity for change in machinery should be allowed to affect the case. That is a mere excuse; there is really no good reason in it at all. It has been pointed out that the seeds must be cleaned from the grain in any case. I would point out that it is often cheaper to handle a large quantity of one kind of commodity than to have it divided up into a large number of classes. This bill will provide for several such classes, and the result will be to add to the expense. I feel certain that those who are feeding the stock will be better served if they can have the bran in its pure state.
The bran cannot be put into the screenings-shorts and screenings is the mixture we are dealing with. Bran will be sold in its purity.

My argument, then, would apply to shorts only, not to bran. I think it is better to have shorts in its pure state and that the screenings be sold for what they actually are. If that is done the result will be more satisfactory to the buyers. They have experience enough to know just what
they are suitable for, and I know quite well that this material can be fed to advantage. For that reason I feel I must support the amendment. I do not know that it has been moved yet, but I understand an amendment is to be moved to have these mill products sold for what they really are.

The debate this afternoon has shown that the country is unanimous in its desire for pure feeds for live stock, and with that view I am entirely in sympathy, but may I point out that there is one way, and a primary way, in which we could help to provide the eastern dairymen and the western breeder with pure feed for live stock that would avoid the mixing of weed seed, and that is not to grow weed seeds. Do hon. gentlemen object to that?
It is utterly impossible.

How is it that we cannot get the good mill feed to-day that we could buy some years ago, is a question often asked. Well, some years ago the millers of this country were able to buy grain that was comparatively free from dirty weed seeds.
Is it not true that the weeds purchased with these mill feeds have been distributed all over the old provinces?

I was just coming to that. But there developed a method of farming in this country, surface farming, what is called in western Canada mining a farm, the result of which has been that the pure virgin soil on which good clean grain used to be grown has now reached a condition through careless methods of farming where it grows a very large percentage of dirty weed seeds. I think all hon. gentlemen will admit that. These dirty weed seeds have been carried over to eastern Canada through the mill feeds and the grain bought, and they have dirtied all the farms so that as you drive through the countryside you notice the deplorably dirty conditions of the farms.
Where did the seeds come from into that grain grown in the West?

I have had some experience. I was brought up on a farm and day after day we were sent out to weed mustard and keep the farm clean. I admit that that cannot be done on a large farm in the West, but I say that that is one way in which everyone oan help to eliminate these weed seeds.
There is another way in the meantime which will help, and it was pointed out by my hon. friend from Oxford county. There is, I am told, a threshing separator that cleans these
Feeding Stuffs Act

weed seeds fairly well on the farm, and if the farmers would help in that way and take out as much of the weed seeds as they could on the farm, there would be that much less to go to the mill. You would really believe to listen to the debate to-day that the average miller Wanted dirty weed seeds. Surely no one believes that. The better and cleaner the wheat, the more the miller is willing to pay for it and the more profit he can make. In anything the Minister of Agriculture can do to compel the sale of pure mill feed I am with him. I am in the business. I represent two firms that pride themselves on pure mill feed?, but I also know that if a man goes out and offers a mill feed with some dirt in it for 25 cents less the feeder is ready to buy the dirt3' feed. There are a very limited number of mills in Canada, and I know them, that are running their dirty seeds into the mill feed.
There is another danger, however, to live stock that in my judgment is far more feared than the weed seeds coming from the run of the mills or from the elevators, and that is the oatmeal mill that grinds out the hulls and runs them into the bran and shorts. I think that is a greater danger to the stock than the seeds if they are ground up fine. I have said enough, I think, to indicate that I am in favour of pure mill feed, and in favour of anything that can be done to secure a larger supply of pure mill feed.
We have had a complaint from some hon. gentlemen that bran was unobtainable, that they could not buy bran at any price. That is true in a degree, and possibly the more restrictions we impose and the more we hamper trade the harder we make it for ourselves to get what we want, for after all there are only a limited number of mills that follow this practice of mixing their seeds. The majority of mills in Canada pride themselves on putting out good mill feed. I will give hon. gentlemen one reason why mill feed is scarce in this country. I have here the records of exports for the ye'ars 1921, 1922 and 1923, and I find that in the year 1922 the total export of bran, shorts and middlings was 729,718 bags of 100 pounds each. In 1923 the total export was 2,300,353 bags of 100 pounds each, so we exported in 1923 almost three times the quantity exported in 1922. I am not stating that the regulations imposed had anything to do with this increased export, but it is clear that the export business was more profitable to the miller and consequently he put his stuff in another market. I am reminded that quite recently we in Canada were very much disturbed over certain regulations that the British government proposed to impose on the 
import of flour to that country. They were going to compel all importers of flour to import along with a bag of flour its equivalent in mill feed so far as weight is concerned. That shows the importance of supporting such measures as will secure to us good feed, but let us not put such restrictions upon mill feed in this country as will make it more profitable for the millers to export their mill feed to another country. I am with the Minister of Agriculture in anything he can do in this matter. I favoured the bill he had the other day for pure bran, pure shorts and pure middlings, and for the sale of screenings as screenings and branded as screenings. If that is done, Mr. Chairman, it is not the Canadian miller who will suffer. It will not hurt his business but it might hurt the man who is growing weed seeds.
There is a difference between the situation in the West and in the East.
Hear, hear.

In the West-there are very large mills situated at Calgary, Medicine Hat, Moose Jaw, Saskatoon and Winnipeg into which the farmer's wheat goes directly and is graded and docked. The millers get the screenings and the seeds absolutely free, with the freight paid not only into their mills but as far as Fort William; it costs them nothing. I say that if this regulation goes into effect it will be absolutely impossible for the western farmer to buy shorts at all, that is pure shorts, because whether the percentage of seeds is one per cent, 2 per cent, 3 per cent, or even 8 per cent the millers will endeavour to get rid of the whole thing, which is a gift to them, as shorts and screenings. With regard to the eastern miller the situation is somewhat different. If the inspector at the head of the lakes is not doing his duty, and is allowing screenings and seeds to go through there, it seems to me the course for the millers to take is to appeal against that inspection. I find there is a provision in the Grain Act for a grain survey board. It is provided that on the recommendation of the boards of trade of Toronto and Montreal respectively there may be appointed for any eastern division a grain survey board composed of such number of fit and skilful persons in each case as is considered necessary. There is also a provision that when the owner of any inspected grain is not satisfied he may appeal to the chief inspector; and further, if he is not satisfied with the decision of the chief inspector he may appeal to the board. I think that is the proper course for the eastern miller to take in this

Feeding Stuffs Act
regard, instead of trying to pass off a camouflaged adulteration. We have far too much adulteration in this country. The minister of Agriculture says that if we do not want to buy this so-called shorts we need not. I may say, however, that time and time again we cannot buy either bran or shorts unless we are prepared to take the flour with it.
Now as to the point the Minister of Trade and Commerce made when he quoted the figures that seven hundred and some odd thousand hundredweight had been exported in 1922.
I happen to have here figures prepared by the Bureau of Statistics and they show 854,829 hundredweight were exported in 1922. But there is another interesting point which the minister did not mention-
There seems to be a difference in the figures. To what period do my hon. friend's figures apply?
To the period ending March 31st.
The figures I quoted were for the period ending in May.

But the interesting point is this: The value is also given and it is $939,910. This works out at 51.02 per hundred weight, showing a value of over 520 a ton. I should like to ask any hon. member sitting near me. from the West or from the East, if he was able to buy either bran, or shorts, or middlings at 520 per ton in 1922.

Will my hon. friend allow me right there?-the explanation will run in line with his figures. These exports are based on the f.o.b. price at the point of shipment. Now, most of this mill feed is exported from western mills so that the figures are based on the price f.o.b. at that mill. To arrive at the price at which the feed is sold in eastern Canada you would have to add the cost of the freight, seeing that the shipment may have been made from Alberta or western Saskatchewan.
That does not quite explain the situation either.
It may not as regards the West but it does in the case of the East.

That will pot explain the
situation in the West where no freight cost is incurred whatever. For instance take Saskatoon or Moose Jaw where the farmers live around the mills. When the feed is sold to them there is no charge for freight to Fort William. The millers grind the wheat there and yet at times we have not been able to get
sufficient feed at any price. The price to us has been 524 a ton when apparently they were willing to ship feed out at 520. That situation is not right. The same thing occurs in the case of flour. We pay very nearly the same price for flour right at the point where it is ground, without any freight on it, that Montreal flour is quoted at. I am glad to receive the minister's assurance on the matter because I did not understand at what point the freight was added, but even with his explanation I contend that the farmers of the West are suffering a great injustice by reason of the price they have to pay for flour and for bran and shorts. If any amendment is moved I shall certainly support it. I should like to see the words "shorts" and "mill screenings" cut out altogether and make it read "pure bran, shorts, feed flour and screenings." I understood the hon. member for Missisquoi (Mr. Kay) to say that these screenings1 had a great feeding value, and that they were even worth more than shorts. If the screenings are so good let the millers sell them for what they are and get all the profit they can out of them; we do not want to deprive them of that profit when the screenings are sold separately.

There is no amendment before the committee. The unfortunate thing is we have not a bill here based on the amended resolution. I have one of the other bills that has been amended in accordance with the resolution. There is nothing for it but to pass the bill in conformity with the resolution, or else get a new bill drafted.
In conformity with the amended resolution?
The amended resolution. If we strike out the word "pure" in subsection (d) of section 1 it will be in conformity with the resolution as amended the other day.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Is it the pleasure of the committee that the word "pure" be struck from the sub-paragraph (d)?

Sub-paragraph (d)
refers to "bran, shorts or middlings when unmixed with other materials." I am unable to grasp what the minister means by proposing to strike out the word "pure." The bill is so ambiguous that I doubt whether anyone can make head or tail of it in its present form. It appears to me as though the object were to enable people to evade its provisions.

It is not necessary
to have the word "pure." The clause was

Feeding Stuffs Act

drawn that way when it provided for a mixture of shorts and screenings. That would imply that there is another kind of shorts that is not pure. Consequently it is thought better to omit the word "pure."

The minister will understand that there is really no difference between bran and shorts except that one contains about one per cent more protein. The bran is gound up fine now and disposed of as shorts. This has been the custom in the past. By adding some of the screenings or lower grade flour, they were able to dispose of the bran as shorts. To-day it is almost impossible to purchase pure bran, notwithst anding it is claimed they are not permitted to adulterate it now but it is ground up and disposed of in this way. I think the minister would be well advised, even at this late date, to alter the bill, so that it would conform with the view expressed by the Minister of Trade and Commerce. The importance of this bill to the live stock industry under present conditions is so great that I think it would be most unfortunate if this session should end without something being done along this line. I am satisfied that pure mill feed would mean more to agriculture in this country than all the money that is being spent for agricultural purposes. I am so firmly convinced as to this that I will venture to make that statement. The millers admit there is absolutely no difficulty; and if you put this into effect you will find the millers will be quite competent to take care of themselves, that nobody will be able to sell weed seeds to the millers and get anything for them, and that consequently it will encourage better farming, and overcome the great difficulty which we have. These weed seeds came into the country in an insidious way, and obtained a foothold before the people realized in many instances what they were at all. I can understand the difficulties they have to contend with in farming in western Canada. In fact, weed seeds were introduced into western Canada and even into Ontario from Europe, but it is only recently that people have become acquainted with the fact, and if it continues for a few years, it will be almost impossible to eradicate them. Better farming will be of immense benefit to the country, and live stock is the basis on which agriculture must be built up.

If the word "pure" is to appear before the word "shorts," it should be placed before every one of these by-products, middlings, feed-flour and so on.
I think we will have to either cut out the

word "pure," or if we leave it in, we will have to place it before each one of these commodities. Therefore, I think it should be eliminated and that the words "when sold separately and immixed with other materials," should be struck out, because that implies the other. Then, after cutting out those words, the word "screenings" should be inserted, because it is a fifth by-product. It appears in the next section. It will then read, "bran, tehorts, middlings, feed-flour and screenings."
If the minister consents to *cutting out the word "pure" and to the other changes, will he allow section 9 on page 2 to stand?
No, that will be cut out, too. The words "shorts and" would require to be cut out as well.
It will have to bo made to conform to the idea of a pure article all through.
The point I am making is that adulteration or misleading tagging or labelling, and so on, is absolutely prohibited.
I think when we get to that, it will have to be made to conform with the idea that every one of the five must be in itself distinct with nothing attached to it.
Before the motion is carried, would it not be well for the officers of the department to look into this matter, and have the amendment made, so that the 'bill will operate successfully.
The worst is past, Mr. Chairman.

I think the consensus of opinion is the same as in 1919. I will read a resolution which was moved by me which was passed by the committee of Agriculture at that time, when my bill was referred to it. It reads:
That in view of the serious results from the feeding of adulterated bran and shorts by adding thereto great quantities of weed seeds both ground and unground annually resulting in the death of many animals and serious injury to the health of others, besides distributing harmful weed seeds throughout the country to the detriment of those who engage in agriculture, this committee would respectfully recommend that immediate action should be taken to deal with this question by passing and putting into effect at the earliest opportunity bill No. 7 an act to amend the adulteration act.
That resolution absolutely prohibits mixing.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Is it the pleasure of the committee that we take this vote item by item?

Before doing so, Mr. Chairman, I wonder if my hon. friend the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding) will make some general explanation as to these further estimates brought down, as they are, in the very dying days of the session when we have a great deal of work to dispose of. I would point out to him that we now have our Main Estimates of $466,000,000, the sup-plementaries of $14,000,000, the construction programme of $28,000,000, the additional sup-plementarias brought down for the year closed of $18,000,000, the bonus supplement of $5,500,000, the liability to be undertaken in connection with the endorsement under the bill which has received second reading of $15,000,000, and the Supplementary Estimates tabled to-day of nearly $15,000,000-making a grand total of $548,750,714. With a very large deficit this year, and with an estimated revenue much less than last year, how does my hon. friend expect we are going to pay for all this-where is the money coming from -what is the loaning programme-how is the country to be financed? Surely we should have some idea where the money is coming from in connection with this vote.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I regret, Mr. Chairman, that it has been deemed necessary to bring down these estimates at a late stage of the session. If that is a criticism, I am willing to admit there is some ground for it. The only explanation is that we have all been pretty busy-I plead guilty to having had an occasional busy day myself. However, apart from that there is nothing in these estimates that calls for any special criticism or any special explanation. The money is to come from those projects which we have disclosed to the House. If my hon. friend knows any part of these estimates which is not fair and

reasonable, it is his pleasure and his duty to point it out to us and, if necessary, challenge the vote of the House upon it. If he is not prepared to do that, I tell him he is not going to alarm the country by rolling up all these figures. Each estimate must stand on its merits. I do not think my hon. friend is going to scare the people at all by his figures. I see nothing remarkable in the situation at all.

Well, Mr. Chairman, I thought we had done something. We at least did our best to criticize the estimates that have already been brought down, but our protests were absolutely unavailing and, indeed, some people think we talked too much upon them. That is all we can do. As I pointed out, there is more than the mere voting of the estimates. Here we have a deficit on last year's operations of $58,000,000-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: My hon. friend knows that that is not correct.
I do not think my hon. friend is doing himself justice when he makes that remark. He got a credit from other years' operations of $8,000,000 on exchange. He taking credit-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I am not taking credit for it. The item appears in the accounts. There is no other place to put it.

He taking credit for that, reduces the total sum of the deficit. There is no doubt about that. He never for one moment tried to conceal it. Therefore my hon. friend is not doing himself justice when he says I am saying something that I know is not so. I do not think he meant to say it. At any rate I am going to think that he did not mean it. We will take the deficit as we have it with the adventitious fund of $8,000,000. Such a windfall will not occur again this year, and even with it the deficit is bad enough. Now in the face of this total vote of over $548,000,000, surely my hon. friend cannot think that one is merely trying to alarm the public by referring to what he is doing. There is no attempt at alarming the public. We are all interested in trying to get things down to something like a normal working basis. The income called for by my hon. friend's budget falls very far short of this huge total. I did ask him in all sincerity where the money is coming from. He is not telling me. I can do nothing more than I have done already in connection with the votes that have been passed-simply register my protest.

Mr. Chairman, the hon. gentleman (Sir Henry Drayton) who has just

Supply-Public Works-N.S.
taken his seat called attention to the lateness of the tabling of the Supplementary Estimates. Last Tuesday, after they were tabled, the right hon. leader of the Opposition asked the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding) to tell him when in the history of Canada such estimates had been tabled during the last week of the session. I have taken the trouble to go through certain records and have found one precedent. In the session of 1921 when the right hon. leader of the Opposition was Prime Minister-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: And my hon. friend was Minister of Finance.

On Monday, the 30th May, 1921, at about one o'clock in the morning, Supplementary Estimates for $23,959,842.14 were tabled. The House prorogued on the 4th of June; that was the Saturday following. That was I think the precedent which the right hon. leader of the Opposition wanted, and he himself is the one who created this precedent when, he was then Prime Minister.
The Montreal Gazette of the 31st of May speaking of the Supplementary Estimates amounting to $23,959,842.14 tabled on the 30th of May says:
The figure is low and indicates a close scrutiny of expenditures. The Main Supplementaries last year totalled $62,000,000 and the year before $36,700,000.
That was not including the bonus for the Civil Service which the leader of the Opposition wanted to include in the supplementaries this year. There may be, I admit, some discussion as to whether these supplementaries might not have been brought down a little earlier in the session, but I do not believe that the strong protest of the right hon. leader of the Opposition was justified in any way, shape or form.

I wish to say a few words
with regard to these Supplementary Estimates, and what I am going to say I am sure is without prejudice. I do not think it makes a great deal of difference to consider this right or wrong now because it has been done before. I notice that the Supplementary Estimates for public works in Nova Scotia are larger than the main estimates for that purpose.
Will my hon. friend allow me a question? Does he not believe in the principle "Let him that is without sin cast the first stone?"

I hardly know where I have sinned anyway. The thing is in bad practice. I have no great experience with procedure in the House of Commons, but just from a
common business standpoint I think it is bad practice to bring down such a large amount of estimates at the end of the session. Among the items that appear in these estimates I might mention the increase in salaries to the deputy ministers. I am not in a position to make any criticism as to whether that is right or wrong. I believe in paying what the work is worth, and if we get efficient servants to do our work we ought to pay them a reasonable sum, but I do claim, Mr. Chairman, that this must have been within the knowledge of the government when the Main Estimates were brought down, and I should like to know why it was not included in the Main Estimates. I want to register my protest against such a large sum being brought down at the end of the session when we have not time to get the information to enable us to criticise these different items. Take the estimates for Nova Scotia for instance. What information have we in this part of the House, at all events, upon which we could offer any intelligent criticism other than that we think this is a large sum of money for the purpose?

I would ask the hon.
member, does he take exception to any specific vote for Nova Scotia in these Supplementary Estimates, and if so which one?

I was just on that point when the hon. gentleman interrupted me. I was saying that it was a large sum of money, and that we were not in a position to criticize. It is a large sum of money to vote without any particular knowledge of the circumstances. Had these been brought down at the time of the Main Estimates we could have made inquiries and got some information before we were asked to vote this money. We are not finding fault if the money is properly spent. You can be extravagant in spending a little, and you can practise economy in spending a great deal. It all depends on how you spend it. I want to register my protest against this practice. I believe it is a wrong principle, and because hon. gentlemen opposite are not able to cast the first stone does not make it any better.
While I am on my feet I just want to say that we are nearing the end of the session, and I think we are all anxious to get through. I do not want to be critical, though I think that intelligent criticism is all right, but I should like to say that we waste a good deal of time in this House in wandering into bypaths and raking up old things that took place years ago and that are of no interest to us in this part of the House at all events.

I am not referring to intelligent criticism. I would like if possible to come right down to business. Let us get on.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I would like to say just a word in reference more particularly to the remarks of my hon. friend the ex-Minister of Finance and the right hon. leader of the Opposition. As far as I have been able to gather, the impression they have sought to convey is that the government in some way or other has sought to delay bringing down the estimates till the last of the month. I think it is important that not only the House but the country should understand that so far as the Main Estimates are concerned, and they are the large amounts covering the business of the government as a whole, the entire Main Estimates with the exception of one item had been passed on the 15th of this month. There has been no effort whatever in any way to prevent full discussion of the estimates. It has been a part of the government policy to begin almost immediately after the opening of the House with the estimates, and distribute them day by day over the session so that there would be ample opportunity for the members of the House to discuss every department and every branch of government. Wihat we took such strong exception to in opposition was that the government of the day, while it brought down it3 estimates at a certain time after the opening of the House, refrained from bringing before the House for purposes of discussion a very large part of the Main Estimates until the last few days of the session. I think if one will look through the records of parliament one will find that the last week or two of parliament during the last few sessions at least- I know that when we were in opposition the end of the session was taken up almost entirely with discussing Main Estimates. Not only that but a great proportion of the Main Estimates were discussed after midnight and until five in the morning. I remember sitting where my hon. friend (Sir Henry Drayton) is sitting now while the government of which he was a member was busy putting through estimates here at night to the amount of millions, and sitting right on until daylight came in through the windows above. I protested strongly, and pointed out that the government was trying to railroad the estimates through the House at a time when it was impossib't to have any discussion and I maintained that if ever the then opposition came into office we would see that nothing of that kind was repeated. I just wish to demonstrate to the House the truth of what I have said. If members will look at the Orders of the Day they

will find there the dates on which the diffei-ent supply has been put through this House. They run as follows on the order paper: February 20, February 23, February 27, March 2, March 6, March 8, March 9, March 15, March 22, March 23, March 27, March 28, April 10, April 11, April 12, April 13, April 16, April 19, April 23, April 24, May 4, May 8, May 11, May 28, May 29, May 30, May 31, June 7, June 8, June 11, June 12, June 13, June 14, June 15.
That is the manner in which the present government has submitted the estimates to the House for the purpose of discussion. They have been distributed as evenly as possible over the entire session, giving notice to members always in advance of what was in contemplation so that there would be ample opportunity of discussing fully every item of supply.
Might I draw the attention of the House to this further fact ? While we were discussing the estimates I do not think there was a single night, unless by consent all round, that we sat beyond eleven o'clock. What I took strong exception to when in opposition was the fact that items would be passed in supply long after it was possible for members of the press gallery to take any record of what was being said or to send any communication to the press of the country as to the discussion that was taking place here. It has been a deliberate part of the government policy to see that the members of the House had the fullest opportunity of discussing supply, that the country should know every word that was said by any member which might be deemed by the press to be of importance in that regard. We have presented our estimates in consequence in that way and all the main supply was completed by the 15th of this month.
The Supplementary Estimates are possibly a little late in being brought down but, as hon. members know, we have been very busy discussing the budget and there has not been time to give to the Supplementary Estimates, until the greater part of the budget was out of the way, the careful consideration which should be given. But let me say in regard to the Supplementary Estimates-and I say it particularly to my hon. friend from Brandon who has just spoken as to the matter of time, we are all anxious I think to get away at the end of this week if possible- if any member feels that in any particular it is going to prevent or even shorten discussion for the House to prorogue this week I hope he will at once dismiss from his mind any intention on the part of the government to

Sup-ply-Public Works-N.S.
have it so prorogue. I purpose to-night to have the House adjourn at twelve o'clock so that there will be no discussion on estimates after midnight, and if we are not through tomorrow by midnight we will rise and continue on Saturday till midnight, and if we are not through then we will adjourn and reassemble for discussion of the estimates on Tuesday. I would like that to be thoroughly understood. The government is not going to seek to railroad these estimates through in any particular. Members may have all the time they wish.
Let me add further so far as the Supplementary Estimates are concerned, we have sought to avoid bringing down in the supple-mentaries items which we thought in any particular would be contentious. My hon. friend from Brandon says that these Supplementary Estimates so far as public works in the province of Nova Scotia are concerned are larger in amount than the Main Estimates, but did my hon. friend take close cognizance of the nature of the Main Estimates? If hon. gentlemen will look through the estimates they will find that so far as new work is concerned, the government both in the Main Estimates and in the supplememtaries has resisted to the very limit the demands that are coming from the different constituencies of this country to start any new public works or public buildings. Here and there there are one or two public buildings which have become an absolute necessity and the commencement of which the Minister of Public Works felt he could not possibly longer delay, but looking through the list one will find that practically all the items for public works set forth in these estimates are in the nature of repairs, and looking through the Main Estimates also one will find that practically all the work is in the nature of repairs. May I point out this to my hon. friend? It is not until the spring of the year very often that it becomes possible for the officers of the Department of Public Works to discover what is essential in the nature of repairs. These are largely repairs to wharves and the like. It is the damage done in the winter that necessitate^ this work. We could let all of that go if hon. members thought it was in the public interest, but it is to save the property belonging to the Dominion that makes it necessary to bring in these estimates. The Public Works estimates so far as the province of Nova Scotia and all the other provinces are concerned are absolutely wanting in anything in the nature of public expenditure for new work. We have I think gone a little too far in that regard. Members of all three groups
have pressed the government hard in regard to necessities in particular constituencies in the way of new buildings, and we have steadily refused. So far as these Supplementary Estimates are concerned while the amounts may be a little larger for the repair work and th* like than in the Main Estimates it is due t' the circumstances I have mentioned. The need for repairs has become more apparent after the winter months, and we refused in the Main Estimates to consider anything in the different constituencies until we had some opportunity of getting further particulars as to these necessities.
In these Supplementary Estimates there are a few amounts occasioned by the legislation that has been passed this session. My hon. friend the Minister of Finance drew attention to the last items brought down to provide for the administration of the Combines Investigation Act. That was inadvertently overlooked. I suppose I am primarily responsible. It was my fault that it was left out of the Main Estimates, and I asked the Minister of Finance to put in a sufficient amount to administer the act which this parliament had assented to.
As to the deputy ministers, I might say a word on that at this moment. There are so far as the increases there mentioned are concerned no general increases in the salaries of the deputy ministers. What the government has done is this. We have ascertained, we have had reason to know, that some of the men who hold these responsible positions in the public service are staying on in the public service to-day resisting offers much more considerable in amount than the salaries they are receiving at the present time.
Well, well.

The government found it necessary to give him $10,000 to retain him, and having given him $10,000 with the extra duties he has, the government felt that where there are members of the public service that have been deputy heads of departments for ten years they were entitled to receive an increase to the extent of making their salaries $8,000. That is what is meant by the increases here set forth. Any deputy who has been at the head of a department for ten years or over is named here for an increase in salary. It is not an increase to the office, it is not an increase to the department; it is an increase to the deputy head who h^p served ten years, simply recognizing the system is general through the Civil Service that length of service be remunerated at perhaps a larger figure. I think if hon. gentlemen opposite will go through these estimates with an eye to the necessity of presenting them in this form at this particular time they will find very little to criticize.
May I add this? Of these estimates brought down at the present time the amount of $5,800,000 is not in the nature of an appropriation for some new work. It is in the nature of a loan. There is one item here of $4,000,000 for loans to provinces for housing advances. Why is that item here? The government in the Main Estimates made it plain to the House that we had felt that previous administrations had made a mistake in voting such large sums of money to the provinces for a number of different purposes to enable the provinces to carry on work which they themselves should carry on. Large sums of money have been voted out of the federal treasury by past administrations for road making, for instance, several millions for aid in agricultural instruction, several millions for aid in technical education, several millions in the form of loans to the provinces for putting up houses in cities and towns. All of this was work which this present government inherited, so to speak, in virtue of the statutes under which these provincial grants were made. They were grants running over a term of years, and if the total of our estimates soems large it is in large part because we have had to carry on from year to year commitments made before we ever came into office at all. We tried to stop certain of these grants from the federal to the provincial treasuries, and among the number we stopped the grants to the provinces for housing loans. We thought it was a mistaken policy on the part of the federal government

to be assisting the provinces in the erection of dwellings in cities and towns. Earlier in the session some reference was made to it and I confess I agreed with an hon. gentleman opposite that it would be much better if we were to spend money for the purpose of housing, to spend it on housing for farm dwellers rather than city dwellers. But we discovered that under the plan previously made a number of the provinces had made commitments with the municipalities that had not exhausted their full amounts to advance them sums which they were expecting to get from the federal treasury, and which they became responsible for in the matter of loans paying us interest on them. When we discovered that we were faced with the alternative of having to say to our friends "well, we will have to go back altogether on the undertaking that has been given by the previous government or else make good this amount." That is why this item of $4,000,000 appears in the Supplementary Estimates at the present time. But I have made it plain, in that once the present year is past further advances shall not be continued. I apologize for taking up so much time, but if hon,. members will look carefully at the estimates they will see that the government has, if anything, erred on the side of refusing to do in the way of public works throughout this country a great deal that is very much required at the present time.

This is one of the fishing vil-9 p.m. lages of which I spoke a few minutes ago, where the fishing business on the Atlantic is carried on by the people who live in the vicinity. The wharf is their only convenience.

Do the local
people take any part in the repairs to these breakwaters? In Ontario, along the lakes, where a breakwater is established, it is paid for by the municipality.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister Without Portfolio
speechtext: I am informed by the official here that my hon. friend from Kingston is hardly accurate about that. In our province, where we require to protect low-lying settlements by a system of dykes, those are carried on under provincial authority, but works along the lakes are carried out by the Dominion authorities.

I am asking about breakwaters. There is no question about protecting low-lying land in Ontario. That work is undertaken by the provincial legislature, but in Ontario a local breakwater is usually paid for by the municipality.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister Without Portfolio
speechtext:
No. My
hon. friend wall find, if he looks at the estimates, that there are appropriations for breakwaters in his province.

There is one in

That is government property.
That is government property too.
The drydock is for the protection of government property.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister Without Portfolio
speechtext:
My hon.
friend has not studied the Estimates. On page 11 he will find two items for Ontario.

In the

What is going to be done with the wharf?

speechtext: It is not a wharf. This work is to raise the level of the breakwater from two to three feet for a length of fourteen feet and a width of sixteen feet. The storms of last autumn and winter practically destroyed this breakwater.
Is this to be done by day labour, contract or what?

speechtext: By contract.
Have any advertisements been issued?
