speechtext: No, we do not ask for contracts until the House permits the money to be expended.

I see there are no less than sixty-eight of these items for Nova Scotia. Are there any wharves whatever in the whole province that are not being either extended or repaired. If so, I should like to know where they are.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister Without Portfolio
speechtext: I am afraid my genial friend from South Simcoe has not visited our province or he would realize that it is an island.

I know it is an island. I do not want a geographical description. I asked the minister: Are there any wharves in the whole province that are not being either extended or repaired? I should like an answer.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: It is not relevant to this particular item.

I submit it is, Mr. Chairman.
M. MACDONALD (Pictou): My officer informs me that we have no data to indicate the total number of wharves in Nova Scotia. If my hon. friend is really sincere, I will get the information and give it to him tomorrow.

I am sincere, for certain
reasons. I do not want to be too critical of the acting minister, but I made a most modest

Supply-Public Works-N.S.
request-I do not know whether this js in order or not, but it seems an appropriate place to refer to it-for a very small expenditure in connection with a government proposition, and could not get $6,000 for it; yet here are sixty-eight items in one single province involving an expenditure of over half *>, million dollars. In the face of this we are told that Canada has not enough money to build a decent road over which expensive government trucks attached to Camp Borden are being damaged daily. The road is nothing but an Indian trail. I am not speaking for my riding or politically, I am speaking for something that is absolutely essential for the ordinary user of Camp Borden. This road is used by thousands of people every year. Camp Borden is a wonderful camp, and I trust it will be kept up. But what startles me is that we find this tremendous number of items here for one province, while we cannot get $5,000 to improve a government property in another province in order that damage which is now daily done to trucks owned by this government may be avoided. I do not blame the acting minister; it is true this has not been pressed upon him for very long. But it has been pressed for a long time upon others; and it does arouse my interest when I see these sums of money being voted here- $5,000 or $6,000, $40,000, $50,000 when we cannot get the small amount required for this much needed work. I am not asking the acting minister to expend a large sum of money; I merely ask for an ordinary gravelled road so that the people using this camp can get in and out and so that the trucks can be used without being seriously damaged. I do think the government should give some attention to a matter of this kind; we should not be called upon to vote huge sums in certain provinces while a small but important work of this kind is ignored. Is every wharf in Nova Scotia receiving attention? I know that Nova Scotia is represented by sixteen Liberals; they are all first-class fellows as far as I know them and I do not blame them for asking for what they think they are entitled to. Personally I should be prepared to support what they are entitled to, but I do not want to support that while the needs of other parts of Canada are passed over.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister Without Portfolio
speechtext: I think my hon. friend is hardly fair in the position he has taken. During the war these wharves and breakwaters in the Maritime provinces were neglected owing to the demands made by war necessities; hence it is that attention must be given to them now. Moreover, last winter was the worst we have had for a quarter of a century, and the injury to these harbours and wharves was very great. As to the road to Borden, the committee will recall that there has not been much disposition these last two years to be very liberal in expenditures connected with national defence or the militia, and the amount of funds at the disposal of that department is not very great. I know that my hon. friend called my attention not more than two weeks ago to the necessity of having improvements made on that road to Borden.
I called the attention of my hon. friend's predecessor to it as well. I have said that I am not blaming the acting minister; nevertheless the records ought to be in his department.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister Without Portfolio
speechtext:
When my
hon. friend called my attention to the condition of this road I made inquiries from the officers of the department, who reported that there was good ground for the complaint made, but that a large vote would be necessary to give the matter proper attention. I gave instructions that the matter be . looked into fully and that plans be prepared for submission next year so that we might consider the question of asking parliament then to provide something for that purpose.

I want to say right here and now that this business of getting extensive plans is a farce. During this recent campaign I travelled on a road, for instance, in the county of Grey from Meaford to Clarksburg, a first class gravelled road, about twenty-two feet wide, on which a motor car can travel fifty miles an hour with safety. That road cost $8,000 a mile. The road to which I have been referring is a mile and a quarter or a mile and a half long. The matter was brought to the attention of the previous minister, not by myself, but by one of the most enthusiastic Liberals in the county of Simcoe. If the country has so much money to spend as is indicated by these Supplementary Estimates, I do not see why we cannot get a work of this kind done. You do not need plans for it at all. It is nothing but an Indian trail at present; all you have to do is to grade the road and put some gravel on it so as to make it fit for travel. In its present condition it is utterly unfit for travel. I say that if these huge sums are to be voted so freely; some expenditure might well be made on the road of which I speak. I ask the minister, are there any wharves at all in the whole of Nova Scotia that are not being either repaired or extended? I shall be pleased to have that information.
Supply-Public Works-N.S.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister Without Portfolio
speechtext: My hon. friend ought not to assume that attitude. I can tell him that there are hundreds of wharves in Nova Scotia that are not being repaired or extended.
Is my hon. friend serious in that?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister Without Portfolio
speechtext: I am serious.
Hundreds of wharves?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister Without Portfolio
speechtext: Surely.
The minister will give me the information?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister Without Portfolio
speechtext: I will get the information.

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext: My hon. friend is exercised over the fact that there is certain work in his district that has not been done.
I am; I admit it.

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext:
That is probably right,
but I would point out that in 1920, when the party he supports was in power, the same item for harbours and rivers in Nova Scotia, No. 490, contained fifty-five items for wharf repairs and extensions and piers. Most of them are not mentioned in this one.
Then if there were 55 in 1920, there is no earthly reason for having 68 now.

I suggest that the minister should read the report of the Deputy Minister of Public Works regarding the necessity for this work, because in all expenditures of this kind the report of an engineer is furnished as to the utility of the work, and so on. What do the Progressives think of an expenditure like this? The Progressives were elected on a policy of economy and retrenchment.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I would draw the hon. gentleman's attention to the fact that he must deal specifically with the item under consideration.
I think it is quite relevant.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: It is not relevant; the hon. gentleman must deal specifically with the item.

This work is not a work for the general advantage of Canada. I would like the minister to give the figures of the expenditure on this harbour for the past fifteen years. It is my opinion that the work is not necessary at all. In view of the large deficits on our National Railways; in view of the heavy debt under which Canada labours, there must be retrenchment. England the United

States, France-all these countries are trying to live within their income. I would like some information about this item. Is this expenditure to be a capital charge or a maintenance charge, and is the money to come out of revenue?

This vote involves an expenditure of 8533,884.60, and the greater part of it is for the repairing of wharves and breakwaters. A few moments ago I asked the minister if the tenders had been received for these works, and he replied in the affirmative. It occurs to me that as this is a hardy annual and as the province of Nova Scotia has grown old in the receipt of these payments, it would be a good business proposition if the government would have a small crew with equipment to go round this island or peninsula and complete the work. That might result in a material saving from year to year.

In the Main Estimates the items for harbours and rivers, Nova Scotia, totalled $293,000. Evidently those estimates were prepared when the present Minister of Railways was in the office, and since the new minister has come in he has brought down Supplementary Estimates amounting to over $533,000. If this is the spirit of the new minister coming in I think probably we were wrong in getting a new minister. We might as well have left the old one there.
I understand that the item that we have not passed yet is this Canada Creek.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: That is passed.
It is not passed. I have been trying to speak for the last fifteen minutes.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The Canada Creek item is passed.

I have been trying to speak to it for the last fifteen minutes. If it is passed I am going to refer to it just the same, and for this purpose. I heard the minister giving some figures. I have heard him imperfectly as the House has not been as quiet as it might have been, but I rather gathered from the quantity of material that was mentioned that the sum of money was not likely to accomplish the work. Now I want to ask the minister a general question in regard to all these items because I think we might just as well have it clearly in the minds of the committee now as item by item. I would ask the minister to distinguish in each instance between the amounts that will com-

Supply-Public Works-N.S.
plete the whole work and the amounts that will only partially complete it. In other words I want to know, and I think the committee would like to know whether these, amounts embrace everything that is to be done or is it only to cover a part of the work. The minister will recognize that it is a perfectly fair question to ask, and if that principle is applied right through by the minister I think we shall save time.
I am not going to criticize particular items because being fortunate enough to come from the Maritime provinces I know the extreme necessity there is there for a great deal of work, and it would not hurt the Dominion very much if perhaps the suggestion of the hon. member were taken and we had a sort of wharf built all around some of our provinces if we could induce the other provinces to make use of our Maritime provinces in the way we would like to be able to do. We still like to feel we are a part of Canada. We do not want to be the only part of Canada, but we do not propose to be excluded from confederation even by some of our too zealous allies. The only criticism I have to make is this, and it reflects on the Department of Public Works, it shows gross carelessness to my mind: There is no reason in the world, despite a hard winter and all that sort of thing, why these items should not have been in the Main Estimates. The information that was available for the Main Estimates was of precisely the same class as we are getting on the supplementaries, and it shows a want of grip in the department that the acting minister is not responsible for but that someone is responsible for, that the House should have to be asking these questions at this hour when these matters might just as well have been dealt with in the Main Estimates.

I understand the hon.
member for St. John to ask the acting minister to state in every case whether the amount mentioned in the estimates was the total amount required to complete the work, or whether it was simply a partial vote and the item would come back to us another year in this or some other form. That is a practice that has been quite common in the last few years.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister Without Portfolio
speechtext: I shall be very glad to give the information. The engineer's report in regard to Canada Creek is to the effect that $1,300 is ample to complete the work.
May I trouble the minister to repeat the dimensions of that work? I might not have heard him correctly, but if the figures were as I understood them 81,300 would not do it.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister Without Portfolio
speechtext: The proposed work consists of tearing down and rebuilding a portion of the breakwater, 40 feet long, 10 feet wide and 21 feet high. In regard to Cariboo Island $6,000 is stated by the engineers to be ample for the purpose of completing the work.

Cheverie-wharf repairs, $1,000.

Hants
county.

general answer. I said I could give the answer in each particular case.

the necessity for going on with this work that is going to cost $15,000 ultimately?

What is the population
of this place?

speechtext:
In addition
to the fishing village itself, in which there are about fifty families, this breakwater serves the whole settlement and district around. There are many people scattered along the shore.

D'Escousse-wharf repairs, $3,000.

We want to
know the county in each case.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister Without Portfolio
speechtext: South Cape Breton.

And whether
this is the final estimate or only a partial vote in each case.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister Without Portfolio
speechtext:
This is to
complete.

Item agreed to.
Dartmouth-pier and dredging, $75,000.

What kind of
a repair job is this?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister Without Portfolio
speechtext:
My hon.
friend has misread the item I think.
No,, I was remembering the remarks of the Prime Minister.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I said most of them. I did not say all.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister Without Portfolio
speechtext:
Dartmouth
is a very prosperous town with a population of between six and seven thousand. It is situated right across from the city of Halifax. This is new work. There is no wharf accommodation at Dartmouth and has not been. Some years ago my hon. friend's friends constructed a railway running from Dartmouth to the eastern part of
[The Chairman.]
Nova Scotia, and through that railway there has been brought to Dartmouth very large quantities of lumber. The opening up of the district has reshlted in great development. The necessity of the work has been vouched for by the people of Halifax county generally and has been favourably reported upon by the engineers. I am satisfied my hon. friends will not make the slightest mistake in supporting it.
I think my hon. friend is right about that vote.

Does the Prime Minister
approve of this extravagance? In the case of all works calling for an expenditure of over $3,000 will tenders be called for, and the contract awarded to the lowest tenderer after fair competition in the open market? Does the Prime Minister approve of this extravagant expenditure on wharves in harbours where there is no business, and where the government derives no revenue? I think I could better justify an expenditure to enable vessels of the Canadian Government Merchant Marine to carry coal from Nova Scotia to Montreal for consumption in central Ontario where it is needed.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Is my hon.
friend asking me a question or making a speech?
Both.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
In answer to
what I gather to be my hon. friend's question I wish to say that the statutes provide-in the case of public works, where the amount to be expended exceeds a certain sum-that public tenders must be called for. Other conditions are also set forth. The provisions of the law in this respect will be fully complied with. I may say further that any public works for which the government asks an appropriation are required in the public interest.

Item agreed to.
Digby-dredging, $15,100.

What part of Digby harbour is it proposed to dredge; also, how much money has been spent in dredging in that harbour in the last five years?
Mr. MACDONALD (Pictou), I will give the information we have. The purpose of this work is to deepen the berth between the two piers so that steamers with a loaded draught of twenty-four feet can load at low water, ordinary spring tides. The area to be dredged is 53,000 square feet. A report on the necessity of this work was made by the regular

Supply-Public Works-N.S.
district engineer. Digby is a very important place in the province. It is' on the bay of Fundy as my hon. friend knows very well.

Is there a government
pier at Digby?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister Without Portfolio
speechtext: Yes.
Was there not a vote in the main estimates for dredging at Digby? I think there was a vote of some kind.

Item agreed to.
Eastern Harbour-improvements, $38,000.
Where is Eastern Harbour?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister Without Portfolio
speechtext:
Eastern
Harbour is in Inverness county.
This is a large expenditure, and, I take it, a new one. What is the nature of the expenditures, and how many people live in Eastern Harbour?

Mr. Chairman, I wish
to say-
I was addressing my question to the minister. He has his memoranda before him and can answer the question.

I think, possibly, if my
hon. friend will grant me the courtesy of allowing me to speak occasionally, I do not take up as much time of the House as my hon. friend does. Let me tell him that he is not going to get me to sit down in the House when I am in order. This expenditure is for dredging Eastern Harbour which is surrounded by a population of five hundred families. There is a large gypsum deposit there and a new industry has been started. A very substantial amount has been spent in erecting a gypsum plant which was closed down during the war. Capital is once more being invested in the industry which is to be operated on a large scale. At present gypsum cannot be shipped from Eastern Harbour until some dredging has been done. Unfortunately we are about fifty miles from a railway. The harbour is a very good one, but there is not enough water at present for ships to come in and load in "onnection with this industry. For fishing and such like needs the depth of water is sufficient. For the purposes of the gypsum industry larger vessels, having a draught of between twenty and twenty-one feet are necessary. That is the object of this dredging. Were it not for this new industry I would not press the department for this vote.

I should like to say that I meant no intentional discourtesy to the hon.
291 i
member. I asked the minister a very courteous question in a very polite way. I do not think there was any necessity for a threat from the hon. member for Inverness (Mr. Chisholm). He has taken as a personal affront a purely harmless question. Now, I asked the minister for a statement and perhaps we had better have it now.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister Without Portfolio
speechtext:
My hon.
friend asked how many people there were in that vicinity, and I thought the representative for the county was in a better position to give him the information.

Can the minister tell us how it happens there are dredging items here, whereas in the main estimates a blank cheque for $600,000 was given to the Maritime provinces for dredging? How is it that the department is not using its own dredges on this work?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister Without Portfolio
speechtext: The general vote for dredging in the main estimates is for the purpose of operating the dredges which belong to the government. They have to be used continuously in certain portions of the Maritime provinces for maintaining access to the harbours. These special votes are for dredging to be done by private parties. Tenders will be asked for and contracts awarded for the work.
Will the minister tell us what we are spending the $600,000 on so that we can be sure there is no overlapping here.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister Without Portfolio
speechtext: I am informed by the deputy minister that that information was given earlier in the session when the main items were under consideration.
I am asking for the information now so as to be sure that we are not voting the same expenditure twice.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister Without Portfolio
speechtext: We are not asking for money for the same purpose twice as my hon. friend knows very well.
No I do not.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister Without Portfolio
speechtext:
I am instructed by the deputy minister that when the vote in the Main Estimates was passed complete information was given to the House as to the number of dredges and everything connected with them. This work is not intended to be done by government dredges but by contract after calling for tenders.

Supply-Public Works-N.S.
I again ask my hon. friend what dredging the government dredges are doing? Why cannot they be employed on this work?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister Without Portfolio
speechtext: I will be very glad to give my hon. friend that information in detail to-morrow.

Let the item
stand until we get the information.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Shall the item carry?
Carried.
That will be a matter for the committee entirely. I have asked a perfectly pertinent question and I have not yet received the information.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister Without Portfolio
speechtext:
My hon.
friend does not apprehend what I say. These votes are for the purpose of dredging other than by government dredges. I shall be glad to give my hon. friend full information tomorrow as to where the government dredges are, the work they are doing, and so forth.
I should have thought that that information would be given before we were called upon to vote the item.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister Without Portfolio
speechtext:
That was
all explained on the main estimates.

That cannot
be so, because at the time on the main estimates we were not discussing this item, and we were not endeavouring to ascertain whether this dredging could be done by the government dredges.

It seems to me that in a town so close to the main centres as Digby or Dartmouth our own dredges should be able to do the work instead of the government hiring dredges from private individuals. Dartmouth is right inside the Halifax harbour.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
If the government
dredge is already employed how can it do the work? The minister has explained that the government dredges were covered by the earlier vote but the amount of dredging is far in excess of what the government dredges should do, and therefore private contracts are made.	.

I think certain friends of
the government in that district own dredges and have been looking for work. They have always been looking for work, and have always received it from this government.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I think there are more
private dredges seeking work in the city of St. John than in the city of Halifax.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister Without Portfolio
speechtext:
My hon.
friend from York-Sunbury (Mr. Hanson) should not be so ungenerous." I am in a position to state that one of the difficulties in carrying out these works is to find dredge owners in Nova Scotia who are willing to tender for the work.

The minister should ask
some of his friends in St. John to tender.

Item agreed to.
East Sandy Cove-wharf, $9,350.
Where is this?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister Without Portfolio
speechtext:
Digby and
Annapolis.
Is this the whole estimate?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister Without Portfolio
speechtext: Yes.

Is this a compassionate

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister Without Portfolio

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister Without Portfolio
speechtext:
I would
fancy myself, for the information of my hon. friend, it was because Mr. Morrison, this gentleman who happened to have this contract, was a Liberal and my hon. friend and his friends who came into power in 1911, did not want to recognize a claim which was perfectly legal.

If that is the only suggestion my hon. friend has to make, there is another suggestion which would be much more in point at the present time; that is, that because Mr. Morrison is a Liberal, and probably a Liberal worker, this government is going round resurrecting an outlawed claim. My hon. friend has no right to make that statement in connection with his engineers. Has he no trust in the honesty of the engineers of the department? speakerposition: Whip of the Liberal Party; Chief Government Whip
speechtext: This work was performed in the county of Cape Breton South and Richmond. During its progress a storm of unprecedented severity occurred along the coast and a great deal of property was destroyed. As a matter of fact buildings were washed off the wharves and along the waterfront. The oldest records in the community recount no such high tide or so severe a windstorm as on that occasion. Mr. Morrison had his work well under way when the storm overtook it. As a result he suffered very substantial loss. It has not been an unusual practice of the Public Works department under both governments to come to the assistance of a contractor who while carrying on work under his contract suffered loss under these circumstances. As to the politics of the contractor, I desire to say, Mr. Chairman, if the matter is of any interest, that he was not a supporter of mine nor a worker at all in the last election. He came to me,' however, after I 'was elected, being a resident of my county. I felt that he had a strong claim to be recompensed for his loss, otherwise he would be in very serious financial difficulties. I beg to assure hon. members that the claim is one which merits the favourable consideration of the committee, and that it is not presented on account of political considerations.
My hon. friend was a member of this House from 1911 to 1917. I presume he knew of this claim during that period?

speakerposition: Whip of the Liberal Party; Chief Government Whip
speechtext: I knew-

Just one minute until I put my question. I would not have anything ruffie the most delightful relations that have existed between my hon. friend and myself during this

speakerposition: Whip of the Liberal Party; Chief Government Whip

contractor enters into a contract with the government and assumes the ordinary risk under it, if by any fortuitous circumstance, whether by act of God or anything of that sort, he loses money, he can then come back to the government for compensation, and that it has been the practice of all governments in days gone by to make good such losses. That is not the practice of the government ;n the other departments. speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister Without Portfolio
speechtext: Lunenburg is an important fishing town as well as a shipbuilding centre. The population of Lunenburg is 3,000. It is in the immediate vicinity of Chester, an important summer resort. I should think that this expenditure would be amply justified. As to the next vote, in regard to Malagash, this point is in the county of Cumberland, where three or four years ago a very valuable and extensive deposit of salt was found. Salt mines have been operated there and large quantities of it are shipped. This dredging has to be done to enable shipments to be carried on by vessels of such size as would transport material of this kind to the larger centres. I may say that information as to the disposition of the government owned dredges may be had by reference to Hansard of the earlier part of the session when the Main Estimates were under consideration. We have no adequate government dredging equipment to carry out the work that is necessary in these particular places. The same thing applies to the vote in connection with Pictou. No dredging of any kind has been done there for twelve years. A great deal of lumber is shipped from that port, and the dredging is necessary in order that the steamers can go in there and take freight. It is only with great difficulty that dredges can be found to do this work. One has been found and has been operating there for some little time. The information with regard to the government dredges my hon. friend will fnd in Hansard.

The trouble is that we cannot find it so that we can put it to any useful purpose now. I am confident we have not any information in Hansard which will enable us to draw any conclusions in the matter.

These items have been before the committee for the last couple of hours and there has been a good deal of discussion which certainly would give the committee the impression that we on this side are not in favour of these items, although we have not expressly challenged them by a division of the committee. I am not selecting the item with respect to the dredging to be done at Lunenburg for any particular purpose except that it appears to be one of the larger items. The government contemplates an expenditure of $40,000 this year on work for which they have an estimate showing that a total of $103,000 or thereabouts will be required. There has nothing been offered to the House by the minister or by others to show there is any urgency in the matter, to show that the expenditure must be made at once. In fact the minister only proposes to do a little over one-third of it during the present year. The objection which we take on this side of the House is this: All these expenditures or the greater portion of them should have been in the Main Estimates.

Supply-Public Works-N.S.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister Without Portfolio
speechtext: Perhaps my hon. friend does not know that we are simply carrying on the work that was started by the government with which he was connected. Money was voted for this work in 1914-1915, 1915-1916 and in 1916-1917, so my hon. friend might well spare his eloquence.

I am not going to spare my eloquence on that explanation. The contemplated expenditure is S103,000 for the whole work. This year the government proposes to expend $40,000. Now the objection which we in this part of the House take to the whole vote is that in the majority of instances these various items should have appeared in the main estimates, which were considered in this House in February, March and April of this year. But instead of that course the government has taken another. It has come down here in the last days of the session at a time when the opposition in this House has had practically no opportunity to inquire into or investigate the proposed expenditure. Now I submit that that is not good practice. I submit it is not fair to the House or to the country. We are entitled on this side of the House to just as full information in regard to each item as is the government. The government may have the knowledge but we have not and we are practically asked to vote these amounts blindly with very little information and practically no intelligent discussion or criticism. I for one at least, speaking for myself, object to that procedure. I have sat in this House and I have heard my hon. friend the Minister of Finance take a similar objection. In the last two sessions under the late government he complained that in the last hours of the session the government was bringing down heavy votes for the expenditure of large sums of money. I know that I shall be met by someone saying: Oh, your government did the same thing. The acting minister has already interrupted me to say, your government did the same thing. Of course, there is hardly a day passes in this House when that retort is not made from some quarter on the government benches, but it is the principle I am arguing for now, and I say the principle is a bad one. I say it is unsound to bring down in the dying hours of the session proposals for the expenditure of large amounts of money involving millions of dollars, which, if voted at all, is voted upon the scantiest information. There is nothing in the nature of urgency in regard to this particular item. For all we know the expenditure of five or ten thousand dollars this year would be just as well as an expenditure of $40,000. It is a
matter of dredging, and I suppose some of it has to be done every year. Why the amount of $40,000 has been fixed upon I do not know, but in order to take the sense of the committee and to test the matter not only in regard to this item but in regard to all the items, because if we do not test it it will be said of us in the future that we did not vote against it-why did we allow it to pass? why didn't you move to reduce it?-if we merely sit here and utter our protests as we have done on item after item that gets us nowhere. Those protests, strong as they may be, are not put down as any opposition to the actual passage of the item, and for all that appears in the records of the House these items pass practically unopposed. Now to test this matter and to take only a single item, but to apply it to all the items comprised in vote No. 504 I beg to move, seconded by the hon. member for South Simcoe:
That the item of $40,000 for "Lunenburg-Dredging" be reduced by the sum of $15,000.
That will leave $25,000 for the expenditure this year.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I do not think we can find any fault with the hon. gentleman's making a motion. I am rather glad he couples with it the statement that he intends it to mean the condemnation of all these items for the province of Nova Scotia. Let it go on record.

I would rather the hon. member who has moved this amendment had not made that declaration in regard to all the other items because I feel like supporting his motion, but I do not fed like subscribing to his declaration. I do not want to criticize unduly, but it does seem strange to me that there is no item for dredging at Lunenburg in the main estimates, while here we have an item of $40,000 for that purpose. For this reason I would support the amendment, but not subscribe to the statement in regard to all the other items because I cannot see the room for the same criticism in regard to them. I might say while I am on my feet that I think it would save time if the Acting Minister of Public Works would answer a few stock questions right away when each item is called.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister Without Portfolio
speechtext:
I really do not know why my hon. friend from South Wellington (Mr. Guthrie) has assumed this sudden attitude of virtue and horror at the government bringing down these supplementary estimates. It is rather a new role for him, though I have noticed a disposition along that line lately on his part. But my

Supply-Public Works-N.S.
hon. friend is not logical in this matter, and he knows it. There can be no suggestion of impropriety about this proposal for dredging at Lunenburg. My hon. friend has sat in this House long enough, and I sat with him long enough to know that this attitude of virtue on his part is largely assumed. It is really not sincere. My hon. friend will not venture to lay down the principle or attempt with any sincerity to argue that there can be any reasonable objection to this dredging proposal at Lunenburg. That port is a little Gloucester in Canada, and there is probably more business carried on there in connection with fishing than in any three or four other places in Canada. There are piers and business places along the waterfront and this dredging work which was initiated by my hon. friend's friends and carried out by them on a regular programme-a contract was let for the dredging, and in one year the work was done by government dredges-is absolutely necessary. Does my hon. friend mean to say that this dredging should not be done? What does he mean by this fantastic theory that this should have been in the Main Estimates? My hon. friend knows that that is not a practical proposal. He is not taking a sincere stand, and why he assumes this attitude I do not know. I think he ought to meet the issue squarely and say that there should be no dredging and repairs to public works in Nova Scotia. If he is speaking for his party let us know it.

As the seconder of the motion I say that there is no such suggestion. There is not the slightest ground for the Acting Minister of Public Works throwing out such a thought. Many items have already been passed. We are entitled to information, and we are not getting it as fully as we should.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister Without Portfolio
speechtext:
What do
you want?

I have asked for some information and it has been promised. The minister challenges me as if I had asked for something that I had got. The minister has promised me the information and I suppose I shall get it to-morrow. With respect to these items that are being submitted to the committee, we say that many of them should have appeared in the Main Estimates, and I have not heard anything from the minister which would indicate that this item in particular should not have been in the Main Estimates. He justifies it on the ground that it was commenced years and years ago. If that be the case there is every reason why the government should

have known about this in January or February and submitted it earlier. No reason has been given why it was not submitted. All this amendment does is to say that this item should be reduced by $15,000. It does not in any way condemn all the works in the province of Nova Scotia.

When are the main estimates compiled? As I understand it they are compiled about November of the year before. I am a little interested in this matter because in the Ontario estimates there is an. item for dredging in Collingwood harbour. That is not new work; it is unfinished work which has been laid over since 1917. However, it is absolutely needed in the interest of navigation in Collingwood harbour where grain is brought down by large boats from the head of the lakes to the elevators. I do not feel that I can support the amendment because the estimate for this work appears in the supplementary estimates. That is because we did not know that the main estimates were made up; we did not know anything about it at that time. Even so I shall be prepared to defend the item when the proper time comes.

May I say a word. My hon. friend the member for South Wellington (Mr. Guthrie) says this is to be a reduction. Well, it might apply to the whole list of items, including those in Ontario, Quebec and everywhere else. It will not do to single out one province and make all the reductions there. This fact should be remembered when we come to deal with the vote of $600,000 for the continuation of the work in Toronto harbour.
Cut it out.
In that case might we not expect the same principle to be applied?
Is not that appropriation being made in pursuance of an agreement. This government has agreed to expend that amount of money and we expect it to implement its promise.

I am not arguing against the expenditure I am just indicating how the argument of my hon. friends might be applied. It is just as well that we should know where we are heading. The hon. member for North Simcoe (Mr. Ross) made a very good point. Every member of the preceding government knows that the estimates are made up in the autumn, and information continues to come in with respect to them month after month in the manner which has been described. If we are going to say that supplementary estimates must be brought in at a certain date after the opening of parliament

Supply-Public Works-N.S.
let us establish that principle some day next session, so that members of parliament will be made aware of the fact and will have ample notice of it. But to begin to establish that principle now, to re-organize the whole system that has prevailed ever since I have been a member of parliament, is something that cannot be done. This practice has been in vogue ever since I can remember. I say frankly that my office has frequently been filled by members of parliament from both sides ever since the session opened. The majority of them do not come to Ottawa until their sessional duties demand their presence. Have we not right to listen to representations from any member of the House on the subject of estimates? The main estimates are made up and closed, as a rule, before any member comes here and information which is needed from members as to any particular item cannot be collected until the House meets. Practically every government that has ever been in power in Canada has recognized that fact. Have not hon. members the right to come and discuss these matters with the minister? I am free to say that I am glad to see members on either side of the House. I do not object to meeting them and I think none of them object to coming to see me about any of these matters relating to my department. When in opposition I have sat up in this House until very late in order to put through estimates at the end of the session. I do not think my hon. friend from South Wellington stayed to help me; he went home and did not remain the greater part of the night. With three or four Liberal colleagues I have remained until four or five o'clock in the morning when my Conservative friends were putting their estimates through, and prorogation took place the next evening.

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext: No, on the same day.

Yes. Circumstances sometimes arise when you have to do these things. The hon. member for South Wellington at first said he was laying down a principle, but he took that back. He said he did not take any exception to the principle of voting the estimates but only to the amount. It is not a principle then which is involved but only an amount. The question here is should we spend $25,000 or $40,000. That is not a statement of a principle. If the House wished to establish a principle the proper thing to do would be to have a discussion early next, session, as to whether the Supplementary Estimates should be brought in late except under the most extraordinary circumstances. Let the question be discussed then and settled so that the members will all know there will
not be any Supplementary Estimates brought down after a certain date. We cannot get away by a vote of this kind from the principle and practice that has been followed by every government ever since there has been a parliament in Canada.

I do not know that my hon. friend is quite fair in his statement of the position in this case. There is no objection whatever to Supplementary Estimates. We have to have Supplementary Estimates, there is no question about that. He is also not quite fair when he says that the estimates are finished the autumn before. Why, the Estimates this year were not finished until after the return of the Minister of Finance from overseas.

My hon. friend knows
that every department had its Main Estimates well advanced, if not actually completed, before the new government came into power.
Sir HENRY DRAYTON; It seems to me my hon. friend did not ask a question, he made a statement.
I apologize.

Everyone who
has been in a government knows that the estimates have to be got out in time and that parliament generally meets before they are printed. This very year parliament was in session and the Speech from the Throne was being discussed before the estimates were printed. You also have to have Supplementary Estimates, there is no question about that either. Nor is there any doubt that the ministers have to meet members of parliament. The only thing we want to do is to find out what the view of the House is on this question. That is, admitting the necessity, as we do, of these Supplementary Estimates, and admitting the necessity of a lot of the things we have heard, the question is whether the Supplementary Estimates are to be brought in at a time which will allow discussion and investigation or not. That is all we are trying to establish.

The conditions along the shore of Hants county are very difficult to appreciate. The tide in the Bay of Fundy rises and falls about sixty feet, a condition which does not prevail in any other part of the country. The result is that the maintenance of wharves and approaches is very difficult indeed, because when the tide is out there may be nothing there but the bottom of the bay. The wharves can only be approached at

high tide. This extension work is to consist of a public wharf along the water front in a westerly direction from the railroad wharf. There are very large shipments of gypsum and lumber made from Windsor. There is a tremendous industry carried on there by the King Company who carry gypsum from Windsor to Bayonne, New Jersey. Hants county is also one of our greatest lumbering counties. There have been grave complaints about the lack of wharf accommodation at this place for a long time. Georgetown-to take over and repair C.N.R. wharf,

What is the
justification for taking over the Canadian National wharf at Georgetown? Is this another scheme to relieve the railway of its ordinary obligations?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister Without Portfolio
speechtext:
I can give
some explanation of this matter having been in Georgetown a year or so ago. Formerly Georgetown was the port in Price Edward Island through which communication wals maintained in winter between Prince Edward Island and the mainland. A very large expenditure involving a very great annual loss was begun in 1912 by the construction of the works at Cape Borden and Cape Tormen-tine and the standard gauging of the railway in Prince Edward Island, and the maintaining of the very expensive boats for carrying the trains over. This wharf at Georgetown was the only wharf available for the people of the town for carrying on their business. It had been built by the railway and was used by the steamers in connection with the town's export business. When the change came in regard to the connections with the mainland and the boats ran no more to Georgetown in winter, the railway simply let the wharf go into absolute decay. It spent no money on it and in consequence the business people of the town had no means by which they could ship by water. The railway had no further interest in it on account of the change in the management. That I think is the situation and the warrant for this vote.
When was the wharf originally put up?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister Without Portfolio
speechtext:
It was constructed in 1905, creosoted piling being used, and it is assumed that such portion is still in serviceable condition. Here is a letter from Sir Henry Thornton with reference to the wharf:
I am in hopes that the Public Works department will see their way clear to take this wharf and shed over, because so far as the railway is concerned, there is practically no business handled over the wharf and there is no justification for the company being called upon to stand the expense necessary to repair the dock. We would be willing to turn the wharf and shed over to the Public Works department on a reasonable valuation, and it really seems to me a public work that should be looked after by that department of the government.

What is being paid to the system for it? It seems to me the Public Works department is taking over a liability. I think they should be paid by the railway for taking it over instead of paying the railway.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister Without Portfolio
speechtext: It is expected by the department that they will be able to get control of the wharf without paying anything to the railway. Sir Henry Thornton states that it is of no further use to the railway.
It is taking over a responsibility, it seems to me. What about this $20,000? How is that divided?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister Without Portfolio
speechtext: The estimated cost is as follows: Renewal of approacn, $10,000; renewal of dock on west side, $9,000; renewal of dock on east side, say $1,000; making a total of $20,000.
That would put it in good shape, would it?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister Without Portfolio
speechtext: Yes.

speechtext:
I am informed the matter is now being investigated and the probabilities point to the course my hon. friend has spoken of being adopted.
Now as to the Raymond-Talbot contract: This contract was entered into on March 21, 1914, with Messrs. Raymond and Talbot, and it was to have been completed in 1916. One of the stipulations of the contract was that it was to have been completed within two years of its being signed. On April 18th, 1914, the contractors were ordered to go on with the work. During the summer of 1914 the war broke out. Early in 1915 the contractors were advised not to go on with the work until further orders. In 1915 the government did not ask parliament for a vote for this work. In 1916 the contractors were to go on with it. They did so during the seasons of 1916-17 but claimed that on account of the great increase in the cost of labour and materials due to the war, and for other reasons, they had incurred certain losses. By authority of an order in council passed on the 4th November, 1918, a copy of which I will send to my hon. friend, it was provided that the department should take over the contractor's plant at actual cost less depreciation, and that the chief engineer should make a careful investigation and report as to the fairest and most equitable final settlement with the contractors after careful consideration of their claim for compensation in connection with alleged losses and reasons for the same.

The chief engineer went fully into the matter and came to the conclusion to recommend a payment of $48,384 with interest. He did this in pursuance of the terms of an order in council passed in 1918.

I did not know, and my hon. friend himself has only discovered this after a great deal of discussion in the House. He passed it over in the earlier part of the discussion, without ever seeing it. I am glad he has given us the explanation, but it took him a long time to do it, although he is himself from Nova Scotia and has charge of the estimates. It would strike anyone as being very extraordinary that after having voted several specific items we should be called upon now for another $25,000.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
It being twelve o'clock
I move that the committee rise and report progress.
Progress reported.

I have the honour to inform the House that a message has been received from the Senate advising this House that the Senate do insist upon their amendments made to Bill No. 84, an act to amend the Industrial Disputes Investigation Act, for the following reasons:
1.	Because the provisions of the act should be equally applicable to employer and employee.
2.	Because the selection of the third arbitrator by the chief justice of a court would remove any possible objection that the person selected might be more closely associated with either one of the contending parties.
Bill No. 251 (from the Senate), for the relief of Flossie May Pinkham.-Mr. Stewart (Leeds).

I have the honour to
recommend to the House that the organization of the staff of the House of Commons, adopted by the House on June 20, 1922, be amended by making the changes set out in the details which I am laying on the table.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I move, seconded by Mr. Fielding, that the recommendation of His Honour the Speaker, laid on the Table of this House, respecting certain changes in the organization of the staff of the House of Commons, be concurred in.

Motion agreed to.
On motion of Mr. Mackenzie King the House adjourned at 12.05 a.m. (Friday).
Friday, June 29, 1923.
